news.title: Elon Musk Says Will Give SpaceX Share To "Every Child In America"
news.text: Tech billionaire Elon Musk said on Monday that he would give every child in the United States a share in his SpaceX rocket company. "Next year, I will give one of my SpaceX shares to every kid in America," Musk, the richest man in the world, said on X."This will be the first of many," he said, without providing details about how the scheme would work. There are around 73 million children under the age of 18 in the United States, according to 2024 data from the US Census Bureau.Musk owns 38 per cent of SpaceX, according to Forbes. His announcement comes after President Donald Trump promised last month to give every American adult $5,000 if his Republican party retains control of Congress in November's midterm elections.SpaceX set the record for the largest initial public offering in history, raising $85.7 billion in June.The company's Starship megarocket reached orbit for the first time in September, a milestone for the rocket central to Musk's Mars ambitions.(This story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is auto-generated from a syndicated feed.)

news.title: Donald Trump issues sinister message as US army detonates stockpile of dangerous chemicals
news.text: President Donald Trump issued a sinister message to Iowa's governor-elect after he raised concerns about the US army detonating the nation’s entire stockpile of a dangerous chemical in the state on Wednesday morning. The US President threatened "I will remember" over Truth Social, after the governor-elect called for "immediate transparency" about the detonation which was fought over in court. The detonation of the bomb-making material lead azide was carried out despite public outcry about potential health and environmental effects, including impacts on the health of local residents, and the safety of water and food. The controlled blast, which took place at about 10am ET, was to dispose of 9,700lb (4,400kg) of the chemical that was stored at the Iowa army ammunition plant in Middletown, a small town in south-eastern Iowa that is home to about 400 people. The explosion risked releasing plumes of toxic chemicals in a 100-mile (160km) radius, but exactly where those toxins will land has changed with the weather forecast. Residents living within five miles of a US Army ammunition plant were urged to evacuate as the military prepared to detonate the unstable chemicals. Lead azide, which typically appears as a white powder or needle-like crystals, is a explosive chemical compound of lead used mainly in detonators, according to the National Center for Biotechnology Information. The US army said that a routine inspection in March at the Iowa facility found that “decades-old, stored lead azide had partially crystallized, making it increasingly sensitive to friction, shock and cold winter temperatures”. The army said that the deterioration had “created a new and growing risk of spontaneous, uncontrolled detonation.” The army described lead azide as a “highly sensitive explosive” which becomes “increasingly unstable as it deteriorates”. Shortly after the detonation, Donald Trump said in a post on Truth Social that “early reports from Iowa are that the Army’s mitigation efforts have far exceeded expectations”. But Iowa’s governor-elect, Rob Sand, reiterated concerns for the safety of residents living nearby, calling for “immediate transparency” following the detonation, in order “to understand how and why this situation became what it did”. In a statement on Wednesday, Sand, a Democrat, said that “there is obviously more testing to do that will provide certainty over time, but for now, federal officials have reported that lead dispersal should be limited, Iowans are safe and damage to property is limited.” Sand also said that he was grateful to the experts on the ground “who did all they could to make this detonation as safe as possible”. Sand's statement was met with contempt by the US President, who retorted in another post on Truth Social on Wednesday afternoon local time. The President ranted: "Rob Sands, the new future Governor of Iowa, is obviously unhappy that the Obama created (2009!) mess was so perfectly handled by the U.S. Army through a flawless detonation, that he’s now complaining about the lead up to the event. "He hurt and delayed the process. Was absolutely no help. Just another politician. He should rejoice at this great success, not nitpick and issue phony complaints on “transparency.” I will remember!" The army released new maps on Tuesday forecasting that the projected path will move south-west of Middletown before extending into northern Missouri. The army warned: “All people, but especially infants, children, pregnant women, adults and children with chronic diseases such as heart disease, kidney disease or dementia, should avoid outdoor activities within affected areas until further guidance is provided.” After the blast the Federal Emergency Management Agency urged residents in the local area who did not evacuate to shelter in place and continue to follow guidance issued by the US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) and other agencies, and to wait for the all clear to go outside by officials. An emergency notification that was sent to phones on Tuesday said that some people within five miles south-west of the plant may be evacuated and warned those up to 20 miles away to remain indoors with windows closed to “avoid airborne lead dust, noise and vibration”. The army encouraged residents who live outside the recommended evacuation zone to shelter in place. The operation was initially planned for last Friday, but was rescheduled three times as public concern grew and environmentalists sued to block the detonation. Trump ordered the military to hold off on detonation pending a court ruling and a sign-off from Sand, the Democratic governor-elect, who does not take office until January. On Monday, a three-judge panel of the eighth circuit court of appeals said the army could proceed with detonating the stockpile, finding that the EPA adequately incorporated safeguards in an emergency permit to minimize the dispersal of dust. Soon after the blast, Lee Zeldin, head of EPA , said that he has been told that the blast “caved inward perfectly”. He said: “When the army was planning its mitigation efforts, there were a number of actions that were taken that included an effort to get the detonation to go… downland and toward unoccupied land within the Iowa army ammunition plant.” “This message that I just received … First off, the air monitors are showing a remaining zero detection, and as far as the blast itself, it caved inward perfectly.”

news.title: China shares flat as markets struggle to shake off tariff risks
news.text:
HONG KONG: China stocks were flat on Thursday in a twitchy session, giving up their opening gains as the Trump administration’s latest tariff proposal and lingering AI concerns kept investors on the sidelines. 

China’s blue-chip CSI300 Index climbed as much as 0.5% in opening trade to bounce off a 17-month low hit in the previous session, before ending flat at the midday break.

The Shanghai Composite Index was little changed at 3,475.46, after dipping as much as 0.2% to hover near the lowest since July 2025.

US President Donald Trump on Wednesday proposed maximum potential tariffs of 20% to 40% on 14 major trading partners including China, in a move to counter excess industrial capacity that his administration has said these countries promote.

A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected the assertion that China is a source of excess capacity.

“Market sentiment is still relatively downbeat,” analysts at Nanhua Futures said in a note.

“Global concerns about AI have not subsided, and although domestic measures to stabilize the market were introduced last weekend, they have had only a limited effect on sentiment. In the short term, stock indices are expected to remain weak.”

Among the biggest onshore losers, the new-energy vehicle sector fell 0.7%, with battery giant CATL down as much as 2.4% to a 26-month low. The CSI Semiconductor Index fell 1.5%.

Hong Kong shares were higher, with the benchmark Hang Seng up 1.9% to rebound from its lowest level since April 2025. The Hang Seng Tech Index was 2.6% higher.

Around the region, share markets cobbled together a rare rally in Asia on Thursday as the latest salvo of US tariffs looked less damaging than first feared, while the Thanksgiving holiday offered a welcome break from the AI pain trade.

The S&P 500 and the Nasdaq retreated on Tuesday due to an AI selloff but finished well off the day’s lows as bargain hunters stepped in.

news.title: US Tariff Plan Raises Stakes For India To Clinch Trade Deal
news.text: US tariff rates announced Wednesday put pressure on India to agree to a trade deal or face a higher levy, leaving exporters and investors with little clarity on the trade outlook.The US plans to impose a 17 per cent tariff on Indian goods, lower than regional peers like Vietnam, Malaysia and Bangladesh. The rate would be hiked to 25 per cent if India fails to secure a trade deal with the US, its biggest export market, according to a statement from the US Trade Representative. Analysts said the US proposal amounts to coercion and creates more uncertainty about the trade outlook. "By deploying a dual-rate structure -- threatening steep baseline tariffs against countries that refuse a pact while offering lower rates to those that sign -- Washington reclaims the bargaining power to impose duties at will and extract unilateral concessions," said Ajay Srivastava, founder of the New Delhi-based Global Trade Research Initiative.The tariffs, which are subject to a public comment process, apply to the US's main trading partners, including China and the European Union, and are intended to address concerns over excess manufacturing capacity. They mark the latest effort by the Trump administration to reinstate its tariff agenda after being thwarted by the courts.India's Ministry of Commerce and Industry said late Wednesday that it had "engaged constructively" during the investigation and that any trade-related concerns should be addressed through US-India talks for the bilateral deal. Negotiators from the US and India have been locked in talks over a trade deal since agreeing to a framework in February. The US trade probes, as well as a recently passed law on Russian oil sanctions, have complicated the negotiations. The legislation gives President Donald Trump the ability to impose tariffs of as much as 100 per cent on the top buyers of Russian oil, like India.With the US accounting for about a fifth of India's exports, some exporters may front-load shipments and diversify further to cushion the tariff impact, while "growing US tariff backlash and upcoming public hearings could still lead to some moderation," Madhavi Arora, an economist at Emkay Global Financial Services, said in a note. The levies would hit labour-intensive sectors, including textiles, gems and jewellery and marine products, she wrote, adding that progress on the trade deal remains crucial. Despite the tensions, both sides have in recent months expressed optimism that a trade deal was close to being finalised. India's Commerce Secretary Rajesh Agrawal said last week that "every aspect of the deal has been more or less finalised," but greater clarity was needed on the tariffs. The latest US proposal "adds to the uncertainty surrounding India-US trade relations," said Manoj Mishra, a partner and tax controversy management leader at Grant Thornton Bharat. The possibility of a competitive 17 per cent tariff rate "underscores the need to expedite bilateral trade negotiations", he said. news.title: Kushner Called Putin a "Historical Figure"
news.text:
Special envoy and son-in-law of US President Donald Trump, Jared Kushner, who is participating in negotiations between Russia and Ukraine, called Vladimir Putin a "historical figure" and a "grandmaster of politics" who "wants peace," reports The Moscow Times.

“People may like what he did, or they may not like it, but he is certainly a grandmaster of politics. He is a historical figure. […] In my assessment and the assessment of Steve [Witkoff] (the second negotiator for Trump), he doesn't just want peace—he wants to try to change relations with America and see if there is an opportunity to start with a clean slate,” Kushner said in an interview with Mathias Döpfner, CEO of the German media conglomerate Axel Springer.

Trump's special envoy noted that the Russian president promised American representatives not to use nuclear weapons in the war against Ukraine.

“Up to this point, Putin has shown restraint. He agreed not to use nuclear weapons, which is obviously very important. He assured us that he has no such intentions,” Kushner stated.

At the same time, he accused Ukraine of dragging out the negotiation process due to a drone attack on Putin's residence.

According to him, in November of last year, the American side began to achieve “certain progress” in the talks, but “at the end of December, an attack by the Ukrainians occurred,” which “set back” the Russian president.

news.title: White House plans cyber overhaul, expands hiring
news.text: Digital Desk | Washington, Nov 26 (IANS) The White House said on Wednesday that it plans to reorganize its cybersecurity teams under two national security councils and expand federal staffing to strengthen protection of government systems and critical infrastructure. Cyber policy and operations teams will be reorganized under the National Security Council and Homeland Security Council “to ensure effective integration across all government cybersecurity programs,” the White House said. The announcement outlined planned organizational changes alongside hiring and security initiatives already underway. It did not give a completion date for the reorganization. The Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, known as CISA, has been exempted from otherwise applicable hiring limits and has added more than 200 people in mission-critical roles, the White House said. The agency expects to add more than 400 additional personnel in the coming months. Separately, the Office of Personnel Management’s United States Tech Force has hired nearly 500 engineers from the private sector across major federal agencies in less than a year to modernize and secure government systems, according to the announcement. President Donald Trump has nominated Kirsten Davies, the Pentagon’s chief information officer, to lead the Office of the National Cyber Director. That office will be integrated into the reorganized White House policy and operational structure, the statement said. The Justice Department and FBI plan to announce another cyber defense initiative next week as a follow-up to Operation Winter SHIELD. The White House did not provide details of the forthcoming initiative. The FBI describes Winter SHIELD as a set of 10 actions organizations can take to reduce their exposure to cyber intrusions. These include strengthening login protections, fixing security weaknesses, replacing outdated technology and keeping protected backups that can be restored after an attack. The White House also highlighted CISA’s CI Fortify initiative, designed to help critical infrastructure operators maintain essential services during major disruptions. It said the administration was working with leading technology companies to test advanced artificial intelligence models, identify security weaknesses and strengthen defenses before attackers could exploit them. The statement cited an existing initiative called the Super Intelligence Force, chaired by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, as part of the administration’s effort to protect infrastructure and maintain US leadership in advanced AI. Another program, Gold Eagle, launched in July, coordinates efforts to identify cybersecurity vulnerabilities across critical infrastructure and expand private-sector access to advanced models, the White House said.

news.title: Yuan holds steady near three-week high despite tariff risk
news.text:
HONG KONG: The yuan held firm near a three-week high against the dollar on Thursday, despite the threat of new US tariffs and weaker central bank guidance.

Spot yuan last traded 0.07% firmer at 6.6636 per dollar, hovering near a three-week high hit during the previous session.

Its offshore counterpart traded at 6.6639 yuan per dollar, up 0.09% in Asian trade.

US President Donald Trump proposed on Wednesday maximum tariffs of 20% to 40% on goods from major trading partners, including China, to counter excess industrial capacity that his administration has said these countries promote. A spokesperson for China’s embassy in Washington rejected the assertion that China is a source of excess capacity.

Analysts say the yuan’s strengthening trend remains intact as the new tariffs would be subject to change and the managed nature of the yuan fixing will anchor the currency.

“Policymakers are unlikely to allow persistent currency strengthening if trade relations with key counterparts deteriorate meaningfully, but importantly the new announcements are subject to ongoing trade negotiations,” analysts at Goldman Sachs wrote in a research note.

“However, a more significant pickup in trade tensions would likely lead to a period of stability in CNY after the recent appreciation.”

Before the market opening, the People’s Bank of China had set the midpoint rate at 6.7096 per dollar, easing from the more-than-four-year high set in the previous session and 441 pips weaker than a Reuters estimate.

 The spot yuan is allowed to trade 2% either side of the fixed midpoint each day.

Elsewhere, the dollar index, which measures the US currency against six major peers, slipped overnight as US equities, showing little reaction to economic data, pared losses, leaving the index well off a 19-month high struck on Monday.

 The dollar index was last 0.1% higher at 103.81.

news.title: Salvadoran who challenged deportation leaves US
news.text:
MADRID (AP):

Kilmar Ábrego García, the Salvadoran national who challenged his mistaken deportation from the United States, arrived in Spain on Wednesday after what his lawyer described as a temporary departure, with hopes of returning to his family’s home in Maryland after President Donald Trump leaves office.

Ábrego García, who has an American wife and child, was arrested in Baltimore in March 2025 and deported to a prison in El Salvador in what an official later described as an “administrative error”. He was subsequently returned to the United States, where he fought the Trump administration’s efforts to deport him again, this time to Africa.

After receiving permission from officials to leave the country, Ábrego García voluntarily departed on Tuesday from Washington Dulles International Airport, accompanied by his wife.

“The government does not decide where my story continues,” he said during a virtual news conference on Wednesday after arriving in Spain. “My family and I will decide our future.”

Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg, a Virginia-based attorney representing Ábrego García, described the move as “a temporary departure” but declined to discuss his client’s immediate plans, including where he intends to live.

“Mr Ábrego García has many options to return to the United States as the husband of a US citizen spouse and the father of a US citizen child. We don’t expect that to happen under this administration, which we know will never give him a fair shake, but we expect that the next administration will prioritise reunifying this family and bringing him back to Maryland,” Sandoval-Moshenberg said.

Ábrego García, who is in his 30s, entered the United States illegally as a teenager. In 2019, an immigration judge ruled that he could not be deported to El Salvador because he faced threats there from a gang that had targeted his family. The judge allowed him to live and work in the United States under Immigration and Customs Enforcement supervision, although he was not granted residency status.

Sandoval-Moshenberg said Ábrego García would decide where to settle over the next two years while waiting out the remainder of the Trump administration. His immigration status in Spain was not immediately clear.

US District Judge Paula Xinis, who presided over Ábrego García’s long-running immigration case in Maryland, ordered the matter dismissed on Wednesday after receiving confirmation that he had left the United States.

US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a post on X that he was “delighted” by Ábrego García’s departure. Mullin repeated allegations that he was a gang member, one of several claims advanced as grounds for deportation and an accusation that Ábrego García has repeatedly denied.

news.title: Trump administration targets China, EU, Brazil with new tariffs
news.text:
WASHINGTON (AP):

President Donald Trump’s administration is planning to hike tariffs on Chinese goods by an additional 20 per cent and raise import taxes on products from the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan and nine other major trading partners.

The new tariffs proposed on Wednesday are meant to discourage excessive factory output in those economies, boosted by subsidies and other trade barriers that the Republican administration says allow overseas companies to flood global markets with cheap goods and put American manufacturers at a disadvantage. The taxes are also intended to help replace the tariff revenues lost after the Supreme Court ruled in February that Trump could not declare an economic emergency to bypass Congress and impose across-the-board tariffs.

The duties stem from investigations into the trade practices of 12 countries, the 27-member EU, and the self-governing island of Taiwan.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said he did not expect the tariffs to rattle the global economy.

“We’ve talked to our trading partners about this — they know what we’re proposing,” Greer told CNBC. “I think a lot of this is baked in, and I don’t think any of these would actually take effect earlier than a couple months from now.”

The tariffs, rolled out the day before Thanksgiving, demonstrate the Trump administration’s willingness to continue imposing tariffs even after voters in this month’s midterm elections punished Republicans by handing majorities in the House and the Senate to Democrats. About two-thirds of voters said that Trump’s policies had made the economy worse, according to The AP Voter Poll, a sweeping survey of the American electorate conducted in all 50 states.

Trump has promised that the import taxes will bring back manufacturing jobs and reduce the federal deficit, but last year’s tariffs contributed to higher inflation that angered voters and led to calls by Democratic lawmakers to require congressional approval going forward.

 Challenge to overturn 

While many Democrats campaigned against tariffs, any effort to overturn them will face major challenges even after they take control of both chambers next year. Some Democrats will likely support some of the tariffs, particularly on China. And Trump can veto any legislation that seeks to overturn the import taxes.

After roughly two years of seemingly arbitrary tariffs imposed on a range of trading partners from Canada and Europe to Brazil, the duties announced Wednesday reflect a key goal of Trump’s trade officials: Pushing back against subsidised factories overseas that can produce and export goods regardless of market conditions.

At the same time, Ryan Majerus, a trade lawyer and former official in Trump’s first term who also served in the Biden administration, said the Trump administration took steps — such as not stacking these duties on top of earlier tariffs imposed in July — to mitigate the impact on consumers.

“This is kind of their legacy tariffs,” Majerus said. “This is the one that most closely encapsulates what they’re trying to do, while also having a degree of recognition of the midterm results of the angst over tariffs.”

The small business advocacy group We Pay the Tariffs, which urged Congress to roll back all tariffs after the election, slammed Wednesday’s manoeuvre.

“Three weeks ago, voters unambiguously rejected tariffs that have worsened the affordability crisis and devastated small businesses,” Dan Anthony, executive director of the group, said in a prepared statement. “Customers can’t afford more price increases, but small businesses can’t afford to absorb tariffs on top tariffs either.”

The levies will be imposed pursuant to Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, which permits the president to impose import taxes and other sanctions against countries found to engage in unreasonable or discriminatory trade practices.

A senior Trump administration official told reporters that the new tariffs would be consistent with the trade deals that Trump reached last year with dozens of countries after threatening severe tariff hikes.

Brazil was separately singled out Wednesday for extra punishment after talks on trade issues stalled. The US is proposing higher import taxes for raw and refined sugar and a new 10 per cent tariff on aircraft, a move that would hit Embraer, Brazil’s largest aircraft maker.

For some Chinese goods, the new 20 per cent tariff will be stacked on top of other import taxes for a total rate of 45 per cent.

Vietnam also faces a 20 per cent rate, pending finalisation of trade talks. The tariffs for other trading partners range from 10 per cent to 18 per cent.

The US and China last year reached a trade truce that is set to expire on January 10, 2027. Greer told CNBC that the administration is proposing a “broad exemption” for US$30 billion worth of Chinese goods in line with the truce.

Trump met last week in Shenzhen, China, with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and plans to host him next month at the Group of 20 summit in Florida, an event at which the truce and issues over access to rare earth minerals and China’s purchases of American agricultural products could be discussed again.

On Wednesday, China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs again stated its opposition while calling for the US to resolve the issue through dialogue. “A tariff war or a trade war serves no party’s interests,” spokesperson Guo Jiakun said.

news.title: Love, Not Spying? US Finds No Evidence Of Chinese Plot Behind Nvidia's Jensen's Affair With Alice Huang
news.text: US officials reportedly told congressional staffers there is no evidence that Chinese intelligence directed Alice Huang to spy on Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang. Current evidence collected by the US suggests their relationship may have been amorous rather than a coordinated play by China. They added that new information could change that or any other assessment. The briefing was highly classified and did not settle the broader questions around Huang.What US officials told CongressThe discussion was a broad overview rather than a detailed intelligence rundown. Wall Street Journal reports that it took place a day after Nvidia's board reinstated Jensen Huang following a pressure campaign from President Donald Trump, who assured the company that Huang posed no national security threat. Officials from the CIA, FBI, Office of the Director of National Intelligence and National Security Agency attended, briefing staffers from the House and Senate intelligence committees and chamber leaders.The China links that remainThe finding does not clear Alice Huang of ties to Chinese intelligence. The briefers said China's Ministry of State Security approached her for information, as Chinese law compels, and that she was in contact with the agency during the affair. The US has no indication she gave the MSS intelligence of significance.The briefing also covered Kang Wei. The briefers described him as Alice Huang's husband and an MSS asset who was often in touch with the agency. People who know the couple have described them to the Journal as husband and wife.Officials still disagreeSome current and former US officials say the affair posed national security risks regardless of what information changed hands, given that one of America's most influential businesspeople was involved with a woman connected to Chinese intelligence. Some insist that passing any information to China makes her a spy, while others say her links to Chinese intelligence are more circumstantial, since Chinese business leaders are often compelled to stay in contact with the country's national security apparatus.Huang's allies take a different view. They say there is not enough evidence to prove Alice Huang is a spy or that Nvidia knew about alleged efforts to smuggle chips to China.Jensen Huang Once Washed Dishes At Denny’s; Restaurant Now Restores Plaque At Booth Where Nvidia Was BornInvestigations continueUS intelligence agencies are still examining what influence the affair may have had, if any, on the alleged smuggling of Nvidia chips into China in violation of export controls. Nvidia's board is also still investigating and was urged to continue by Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton.Alice Huang was a top executive at Megaspeed International, an Nvidia partner accused of smuggling Nvidia chips to China. She is being investigated as part of two Justice Department probes into chip diversion, covering Megaspeed and another company, Super Micro.What comes nextLawmakers are seeking more information about the relationship. Huang is scheduled to be interviewed privately by three House committees, including the House Intelligence Committee, on Tuesday, and to testify publicly before the Senate Banking Committee on December 3. news.title: Major economies balk at new US tariffs over 'unfair' trade
news.text: WASHINGTON: Major economies from China to the EU hit out at proposed new US tariffs after Washington concluded its months-long probe into alleged excess production, potentially opening a new phase in trade tensions with both allies and foes alike.The new tolls, which follow an investigation launched days after the Supreme Court struck down President Donald Trump's previous duties, range up to 20 percent and face a period of public comment before taking effect, at the earliest in January.The levies target some of the United States' largest trading partners, with China, the European Union, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand and Vietnam in the crosshairs.Some, such as Japan, denied having excessive production."Japan does not have any non-market policy practices or structural excess production capacity... It is regrettable that a proposed measure targeting Japan has been announced in spite of this," the country's top government spokesman Minoru Kihara said.A senior US official, speaking on condition of anonymity, noted that the proposals sought to take existing trade deals into account.China is among those facing a 20-percent tariff, but US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the new levies were within the bounds of existing trade negotiations with Beijing."China understands that we're going to have some level of tariffs. This falls within that understanding," he told US broadcaster CNBC, adding that Washington was offering China exemptions on around $30 billion of goods..US proposes new tariffs on 14 nations; India faces levy of up to 25%, China hit hardest.Real concernThe European Union said it rejected the premise of new tariffs and expected the United States to stick by a deal struck last year."The EU and the US share a real concern about global overcapacity, much of it state-driven and concentrated in third countries. We regret the lack of joint action," European Commission spokesman Olof Gill said.China's foreign ministry, responding to a question about the new levies before they were officially announced, warned Washington not to engage in "tariff wars and trade wars."And Singapore said on Thursday it was "very disappointed" with the proposals and denied it was protecting its domestic market or subsidizing manufacturing.Vietnam also faces a 20-percent tariff; Cambodia and Indonesia 18 percent; and India 17 percent, according to the USTR's office.The EU, South Korea and Taiwan, which have signed trade deals with the United States, will see tariffs broadly capped at 15 percent.In a separate announcement, the USTR also proposed additional tariffs on goods from Brazil, including aircraft, over alleged inaction on addressing US trade concerns.The Brazilian president's office called the measures "unacceptable" and said Brasilia would "not yield to this type of threat."Trump's tariffs have targeted Washington's friends and foes alike, and are part of a push in his second term to remake global trade by forcing countries to buy US products or produce their goods in the country.Overcapacity concerns affect a range of sectors, from batteries to cement and chemicals to processed food, the senior US official said..25% proposed US tariffs: India rejects excess capacity charge, seeks early trade deal.Hollowing outThe duties could add further pressure on US businesses already squeezed by earlier tariffs, with firms now likelier to pass on expenses to consumers already frustrated with the high cost of living.Affordability was a key issue in this month's US midterm elections, which saw Trump's Republican Party swept out of power in both chambers of Congress by Democrats.The announcement came as data showed the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge at a three-year high in October, adding to pressure to hike interest rates.Trade lawyer Ryan Majerus told AFP that he expected this probe to be among "the most important" actions for the Trump administration, given its underlying concern that factories with excess capacity start operations abroad and "never get turned off, even if there's no demand."This potentially leads to an oversupply of goods, depressed prices and a "hollowing out" of US manufacturing, he added.While the US Supreme Court struck down Trump's global tariffs news.title: Kim Jong Un Makes Rare Show Of Nuclear Warheads After Snubbing Trump Talks
news.text: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un inspected atomic warheads and a plant making fissile material for bombs, pledging never to waver from his country's status as a nuclear-armed state after snubbing President Donald Trump's overtures for talks.In his most direct comments aimed at the US since Trump floated a meeting with Kim during a trip to Asia last week, the North Korean leader accused Washington of approving South Korea's push to acquire a nuclear-powered submarine, state media reported Thursday.The official Korean Central News Agency also released pixelated photos of Kim inspecting an array of warheads, a rare public display of the weapons accompanied by rhetoric underscoring the regime's reliance on nuclear arms for its security."Our nuclear capability has now become a reality," Kim said, according to KCNA, adding that North Korea will "never change" its status as a nuclear weapons state and views the arsenal as essential to defending against hostile forces."This is the greatest number of nuclear warhead types we've seen in a single North Korean image," Ankit Panda, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Endowment for International Peace, wrote in an analysis. Metal casings of five separate designs were displayed, including a "super-large" nuclear warhead Pyongyang has repeatedly alluded to in recent years, he said.Kim appears to be nearing what he considers sufficient quality and quantity for his nuclear arsenal, Panda wrote, adding that the North Korean leader "is pretty clearly not interested in anything resembling denuclearization, but does appear to be interested in trying to get a fundamentally new bargain with the United States."North Korea also showed Kim inspecting what appeared to be a facility to enrich uranium for weapons. This came about a week after Rafael Grossi, the head of the United Nations nuclear watchdog, said Pyongyang has been expanding its uranium-enrichment facilities to make bomb-grade material and called it a serious concern.Trump met Kim three times during his first term as president and said he wanted to meet the North Korean leader again during his Asia trip. No meeting took place and the US president later said in an interview with the New York Post that Kim did not ignore him but that it was "not really the right time." Kim's regime produced only about six bombs' worth of fissile material annually during Trump's first term, according to estimates from weapons experts. During that time, Trump's relationship with Kim shifted from brinkmanship to bromance - prompting the US president to declare North Korea was no longer a nuclear threat.Kim, however, expanded nuclear production and developed more missiles capable of delivering atomic weapons, and the regime can now produce about 12-15 bombs' worth of fissile material a year, experts have said.Without directly referring to Trump's overtures, Kim said Pyongyang was in no rush to negotiate. "It is enough for us to have the strength to contain and control the nuclear threats by the enemies and to retaliate in a worst-case scenario, and we will never seek the recognition and approval of anyone," Kim said.South Korea's Ministry of National Defense said it views "with great seriousness North Korea's stated intention to expand the operational use of tactical nuclear weapons on the Korean Peninsula," calling on Pyongyang to cease its nuclear program.(Except for the headline, this story has not been edited by NDTV staff and is published from a syndicated feed.)
news.summary: Kim Jong Un accused Washington of approving South Korea's push to acquire a nuclear-powered submarine.

news.title: Kim Jong Un calls for wider deployment of North Korea’s tactical nuclear weapons
news.text:
North Korean leader Kim Jong Un called for deploying tactical nuclear weapons for a broader range of military missions and said the country was steadily expanding its capacity to produce nuclear material, state news agency KCNA reported Thursday.

Kim Jong Un made the remarks while inspecting nuclear material production and weapons research facilities. 

Kim Jong Un dismissed calls for denuclearization and said Pyongyang would treat any attempt to deny its status as a nuclear-armed state as a declaration of war. North Korea enshrined its nuclear weapons policy in its constitution in 2023. 

The leader described the arsenal as essential to the country’s security and said he would never give it up.

North Korea has conducted six nuclear tests since 2006, the most recent and most powerful in 2017. The size of its arsenal remains uncertain. South Korea’s defense minister said in August that private researchers estimated Pyongyang had between 80 and 120 warheads, a figure he said could not be officially confirmed.

Kim’s comments come as US President Donald Trump has sought to reopen talks with Pyongyang. The Wall Street Journal reported that Trump tried to reach Kim through diplomatic channels and later sent him a letter. A possible meeting during Trump’s trip to Asia did not materialize, with Kim reportedly setting terms Washington could not accept.

Trump and Kim met three times during Trump’s first term, most recently at the inter-Korean border in June 2019. Those talks failed to resolve disagreements over dismantling North Korea’s nuclear program. Washington has reportedly considered seeking limits on nuclear and ballistic missile testing while dropping its explicit demand that Pyongyang dismantle the program. Such a move would mark a major shift in US policy.

news.title: Why the US Army detonated tonnes of toxic chemical near farmland
news.text:
The US Army has destroyed America's entire stockpile of a toxic bomb-making material in a controlled explosion in Iowa.

The detonation took place at 9am on Wednesday, local time, in Middletown, Iowa, after a public outcry.

Here is what to know about the operation.

Why was the stockpile blown up?

In 2009, stockpiles of lead azide (an explosive chemical once used to detonate military munitions) were moved from military bases across the country to the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant for long-term storage.

The army said in March it had discovered the lead azide had crystallised and become unstable.

Officials said the compound would eventually explode on its own if left unaddressed, and chemically neutralising or relocating the storage drums was not possible.

With winter approaching, the army said the situation was becoming more urgent, as cold temperatures risked a spontaneous explosion.

Leaders decided a controlled detonation of the more than four tonnes of chemical was the safest course of action.

Why were people concerned?

The detonation was likely to create a plume of lead-laced dust that could travel up to 80 kilometres south-west of the military installation, to the north-east corner of the neighbouring state of Missouri.

Lead is a toxic heavy metal that can cause long-term health problems in humans and animals.

There is no safe level of exposure, particularly for children and pregnant people, Patrick O'Shaughnessy, a public health professor at the University of Iowa, said, because lead can inhibit development of the brain and its cognitive abilities.

Environmental groups had sued in hopes of blocking the explosion, and while it was temporarily halted by orders from an appeals court and US President Donald Trump, it was ultimately allowed to go ahead.

Dr O'Shaughnessy said immediate risks from inhaling the lead particles would likely be mitigated if people sheltered from the dust plume as it passed over them.

Nearby towns were voluntarily evacuated ahead of the detonation, and residents in wider affected areas were advised to keep their windows and doors closed for 24-48 hours after the detonation.

But Dr O'Shaughnessy said long-term risks could come from lead dust settling on homes, farms and in the environment, where it would not break down further.

Iowa is one of the US's biggest farming states, with agriculture estimated to make up about 20 per cent of its economy.

Officials estimated about 350 farms could be impacted by the fallout.

Farmers and ranchers worried about protecting their crops and herds.

While the state's Department of Agriculture and Land Stewardship recommended cattle farmers move their livestock, feed and equipment to alternate locations or indoors to avoid direct exposure, it acknowledged that in some places, that would not be feasible.

"I don't think lead danger goes away any time soon," said Lucy Giehl, who lives nearby in West Burlington.

"It seems someone might have thought about all of this a little sooner before it came to this."

Was the detonation contained?

To contain the blast, earthen barriers were built around a pair of bunkers holding 68 barrels of lead azide.

Foam and water were used to tamp down any dust, as witnesses reported two white plumes rolling high into the air before quickly dissipating.

The Environmental Protection Agency said in a statement after the detonation that its air monitors were detecting zero airborne lead throughout the region.

But researchers said the final results aren't in yet.

Andrew Whelton, an environmental engineering professor at Purdue University, said while the early results were promising, samples still needed to determine whether there were any health risks.

"This should take days to weeks," he said.

The EPA said it would test air, land and water samples in the coming days and deploy remediation efforts "where necessary".

But some residents told Reuters they had gathered their own soil samples for independent testing.

Doug Seyb, a livestock farmer from Donnellson, was still concerned about the accuracy of EPA air monitors.

"All of these cows are pregnant, and we just cross our fingers that we don't have deformed calves and stillborns," he said.

Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand said he was grateful to experts for limiting the lead dispersal, but the lead-up "should never have been so chaotic and unclear". 

"Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared," he said. 

"There must be immediate transparency to understand how and why this situation became what it did."

ABC/AP/Reuters
news.summary: The US Army destroyed America's entire stockpile of a toxic bomb-making material in a controlled explosion in Iowa on Wednesday. Here's why.

news.title: Trump administration ‘rules out US troops and bases in Ukraine as part of post-war security guarantees’
news.text:
US negotiators have privately ruled out the possibility of maintaining American troops and military bases in post-war Ukraine, according to a report. 

Sources close to the negotiations told the Kyiv Independent that the Trump administration was not willing to put boots on the ground in Ukraine despite Kyiv’s request, as part of a wide-ranging package of security guarantees. 

Ukraine fears that a lack of support from other countries to deter Russia will only encourage another future invasion. 

Washington’s position has reportedly confused Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky, who has expressed concern over what American safety guarantees would look like if they do not involve a presence on the ground. 

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner discussed security guarantees at a 19 November summit with European leaders. At the summit, leaders discussed a safety protocol similar to Nato’s Article 5 collective defence commitment. 

However, Zelensky has now said he is yet to hear what exactly this would look like. 

"It's not clear yet, because we still don't have a clear answer, a full answer, about what this collective group would be, how it would defend us, and whether this group would be ready to repel the aggressor," he told the Kyiv Independent.

"This has to be on paper. So far, I haven't seen any such steps on paper."

This report comes after President Donald Trump called Russian President Vladimir Putin his “friend” several times following a joint summit with China in Shenzhen on nuclear risks and petroleum products. 

Trump also referred to the US, Russia and China as “The Great Powers” on Truth Social. 

According to people familiar with the peace negotiations, the US may be reluctant to put these guarantees on paper, as any peace deal would have to be approved by Russia as well. Putin is unlikely to sign a deal which would see Nato troops on Russia’s border. 

Heavy casualties continue on the ground despite ongoing diplomatic efforts to end the conflict. 

Two Ukrainians were killed and more than 40, including an infant, were injured in Russian strikes on an apartment building in southern Ukraine on Tuesday. 

Nato leaders have also pledged increased support to Poland after two Russian missiles and a drone entered Polish airspace on Friday in an incident which Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk said did not appear to be an accident.
news.summary: President Trump embraced Putin as a ‘friend’ at a trilateral summit with Xi Jinping last week in scenes that caused concern in Europe

news.title: United States proposes new tariffs on China and European Union
news.text:
United States proposes new tariffs on China and European Union

The United States is considering additional tariffs on goods from 14 trading partners, including China and the European Union.

The US Trade Representative announced the proposed measures after investigating 16 trading partners for alleged unfair trade practices.

Mexico and Norway appear likely to avoid additional tariffs.

China would face the largest increase, with an additional 20 percent tariff on its goods.

Chinese imports are already subject to a 25 percent tariff, according to Reuters.

The US administration says the measures are intended to counter industrial overproduction by foreign countries.

The proposed rate for European goods has not been disclosed.

The United States and EU previously agreed that tariffs on European products would not exceed 15 percent.

An European Commission spokesperson said Wednesday that the EU expected the US to comply with that ceiling, including when new measures are combined with existing tariffs.

President Donald Trump introduced broad punitive tariffs in April 2025, but the US Supreme Court overturned them in February 2026.

Trump subsequently imposed a general 10 percent tariff on EU goods.

Peter Bay Kirkegaard of the Confederation of Danish Industry expects any additional EU tariff to be limited to 5 percent.

He warned that a higher rate would violate the US-EU agreement.

The proposed tariffs would also target India, Japan, Malaysia, Switzerland, South Korea, Taiwan and Vietnam, an unnamed senior US official told Reuters.

news.title: Trump, NATO chief urge Russia not to ‘expand’ Ukraine war
news.text:
West Palm Beach: US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte urged Russia not to “expand the war” in Ukraine, in a joint statement issued Wednesday after meeting in Florida.

The “outstanding” and “very impactful” meeting focused on the wars in Ukraine and Iran, said the statement issued by the White House after the closed-door talks at Trump’s Mar-a-Lago resort.

“We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible,” the statement added.

The joint appeal by Trump and Rutte comes despite the US leader describing Russian President Vladimir Putin as “my friend” during a meeting in China last week.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has taken issue with Trump’s comments on Putin.

“For us, he is a killer,” Zelensky told CNN.

Rutte was asked about Trump’s comments in an interview with Fox News’ “Fox & Friends” on Wednesday.

“What President Trump is doing, also in the meeting in Shenzhen, is testing Putin,” the NATO secretary general said.

“How serious is he? Is he willing to come to the negotiating table? Is he willing to really engage in talks.

“So let’s keep the pressure on. I think it is working, and we have to keep that going.”

Trump, accused by critics of siding with Moscow over Kyiv, said following his meeting with Putin that the Russian leader wants to see the war end by “diplomatic means.”

The Florida meeting comes as European nations have expressed a desire to join preliminary talks that have so far only included Ukraine, the United States and Russia.

Rutte said any agreement is going to have to include security guarantees for Ukraine.

“When the war ends, either with a peace deal, preferable, or if not possible, a long-term ceasefire, we need to make sure that Ukraine has the security guarantees going forward,” he said.

“But the most important thing here,” Rutte added, “is that we have to make sure that Ukraine has what it needs to keep the fight going, being so successful and putting that maximum pressure on the Russians.”

Trump and Rutte also discussed increasing defense spending, which the US president has pressed European powers to do, the joint statement said.

The Florida talks also came as Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth is expected to announce in coming weeks a review of the US force presence in Europe.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte have issued a statement urging Russia not to expand the conflict in Ukraine, following a meeting in Florida.

news.title: Wrongly deported Salvadoran man arrives in Spain from US
news.text:
MADRID - A Salvadoran man who was wrongly deported from the United States, placing him at the centre of a row over President Donald Trump's crackdown on migrants, arrived in Madrid on Wednesday, AFP reporters witnessed.Kilmar Abrego Garcia's case became a flashpoint in the 2025 political battle over Trump's mass deportations, raising questions about migrants' ability to challenge their orders to leave and the government's willingness to respect court decisions.Wearing sunglasses and a baseball cap, he did not speak to reporters who surrounded him as he made his way to a vehicle at Madrid airport, according to AFP journalists at the scene."While details remain private, Kilmar is planning on hosting various international speaking engagements, with stops planned in different countries," We Are CASA, a US immigrant advocacy group which has been supporting him, said in a statement.The Trump administration wanted to deport Abrego Garcia on Tuesday "handcuffed, on an ICE flight bound for Liberia", his lawyer Simon Sandoval-Moshenberg told reporters at Madrid airport, referring to the federal immigration agency.Separate from the criminal proceedings, ICE agents once more detained Abrego Garcia and sought to deport him to Uganda and later Liberia

"And what happened? He walked out a free man, without any restrictions, without shackles on his feet. He left for the country of his choosing, and he did so on a commercial flight, alongside everyone else," Sandoval-Moshenberg added, calling it "a victory".US Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, who oversees immigration enforcement, said he was "delighted" that Abrego Garcia, 31, "has self-deported from the United States to Spain".'Free man' 

Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident married to an American woman, was among more than 200 people sent to El Salvador's notorious Center for Terrorism Confinement (CECOT) mega-prison in March of last year.|He had been living in the United States under protected legal status since 2019, when a judge ruled he should not be deported because he could be harmed in his home country.Justice Department lawyers admitted at the time that Abrego Garcia had been wrongly deported due to an "administrative error".He returned to the United States last June, with his case becoming a lightning rod for opponents of Trump's efforts to carry out mass deportations.After his return, Abrego Garcia was detained again and charged with human smuggling in the southern state of Tennessee. The case was later dismissed.Separate from the criminal proceedings, ICE agents once more detained Abrego Garcia and sought to deport him to Uganda and later Liberia."A year and a half ago, the Trump Admin wanted to leave Kilmar to rot in a Salvadoran gulag," Maryland Senator Chris Van Hollen, who visited Abrego Garcia at the CECOT, said in a statement."Today, he is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man -- unharmed and with dignity."

news.title: Ireland and its pharma sector remains in Donald Trump’s spotlight
news.text:
Companies selling to the US market will be going through the detail of the latest tariff announcement from the White House. The devil is always in the fine detail with tariffs, but the 15 per cent cap agreed with the European Union as part of the deal reached last year will remain, meaning for many exporters the impact should be limited at most. 

It appears that pharma exports from Ireland – which face no tariffs – will remain excluded. The White House has done deals with the big pharma companies involving more investment in the US. It may be early January before there is full clarity on all sectors.

There are two main messages for Ireland. One is that Donald Trump is sticking to his US tariff policies, despite his midterm elections loss, which was due, in part, to the inflationary pressures these created.

The United States supreme court ruled in early 2026 that many of the tariffs Trump had imposed were illegal. He found a temporary workaround this year and set in train a so-called section 301 investigation of unfair trade practices in trading partners. This was designed to give legal weight to permanent tariffs, without recourse to Congress. 

Having “found” what it was looking for in terms of allegedly unfair practices, the latest tariff announcement followed. Whether it is all legally sound remains to be seen. 

The second thing to note is how often Ireland is mentioned in the document of findings against the EU. As the EU country with the second highest trade surplus with the US in 2025 – after Germany – Ireland is front and centre in the report, which points to the State’s long record of attracting US investment and promoting exports. In the world of Trumpenomics, having a trade deficit with another country is seen as “losing” and being taken advantage of. 

Noting Ireland’s $102.1 billion (€93 billion) exports of pharma drugs and medicines to the US last year, the report warns of the risks it believes this creates for the US. If any disruptions hit the market for these vital products, the US could face shortages or delays, which “would threaten the US health industry and consumers”. 

It is not clear what this means for future policy. But Trump’s White House clearly remains perturbed by Ireland operating as an offshore hub for US pharma.

news.title: Trump, Rutte Warn Russia Against Escalation, Call for Swift Peace in Ukraine
news.text:
US President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte issued a joint warning to Russia on Wednesday, Nov. 25, urging Moscow to refrain from any actions that could widen its war against Ukraine and stressing the need to secure peace as rapidly as possible.

In a joint statement released by the White House following their closed-door meeting at Mar-a-Lago, Trump and Rutte described their discussions as an “outstanding meeting,” identifying Russia’s war against Ukraine and the conflict in Iran as the principal subjects of their talks.

“We also discussed the ⁠importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, ​expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution ​to the war as rapidly as possible,” the leaders said in their statement.

Trump and Rutte also reviewed what they described as the “record setting achievements” of NATO’s last two summits in The Hague and Ankara, emphasizing the importance of further increasing defense expenditure and investment in defense production, both in the US and across the alliance.

Rutte says Trump is testing Putin

Ahead of the meeting, Rutte defended Trump’s diplomatic engagement with Putin, saying the US president was testing the Russian leader’s willingness to end the war.

The NATO chief also reiterated that any settlement must include credible security guarantees for Ukraine, regardless of whether the fighting ends through a comprehensive peace agreement or a long-term ceasefire.

The Mar-a-Lago meeting came less than a week after Trump held unprecedented trilateral talks with Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in Shenzhen, which failed to deliver a ceasefire in Ukraine.

Speaking after the Shenzhen meeting, Putin publicly rejected a ceasefire, while Trump subsequently assured European leaders that he believed Moscow was serious about peace negotiations.

Meanwhile, Trump’s negotiator Jared Kushner acknowledged in an interview released Wednesday that Putin remained uninterested in accepting a ceasefire before a broader settlement.

President Volodymyr Zelensky has repeatedly insisted that an unconditional ceasefire must precede negotiations over a comprehensive peace agreement.
news.summary: US President Donald Trump and NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte warned Russia against actions that could expand its war against Ukraine following talks at Mar-a-Lago. The two leaders stressed the importance of securing a peaceful resolution as rapidly as possible. They also reaffirmed the need to increase defense spending and investment in defense production across NATO. The meeting followed Trump’s talks with Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping in China.

news.title: GTRI calls US tariff under Section 301 coercive bargaining tool, urges India to reject it
news.text: New Delhi The Global Trade Research Initiative (GTRI) has urged India to reject a proposed trade deal with the United States under the Section 301 excess-capacity investigations, alleging that Washington is using the threat of steep tariffs to extract one-sided trade concessions from its trading partners. In its report, GTRI said the proposed tariffs by US President Donald Trump effectively revive the reciprocal tariff regime under a different name, with a dual-rate structure designed to pressure countries into signing trade agreements. "The new tariffs proposed by US President Donald Trump under Section 301 excess-capacity investigations recreate the reciprocal-tariff regime under a new name," the report said. According to GTRI, the proposed framework offers lower tariff rates to countries that enter into trade agreements while imposing higher baseline duties on those that refuse to sign a pact. It argued that such an arrangement allows Washington to secure trade concessions without addressing the underlying concerns over industrial overcapacity. The report noted that India faces proposed tariffs of up to 25 per cent, which could be reduced to 17 per cent if a trade agreement is finalised. In comparison, Bangladesh faces a proposed deal rate of 18 per cent, while Vietnam and China face rates of 20 per cent. GTRI described the proposed 17 per cent rate for India as a calculated attempt to offer the country a marginal tariff advantage over competing economies rather than an objective assessment of industrial capacity. "The offering of India a 17% deal rate (versus 25% without a pact) is a calculated bait designed to show a marginal 1%-3% tariff edge over rivals like Bangladesh, Vietnam, and China," the report stated. The investigation has flagged potential excess capacity or export surpluses in seven Indian sectors, including solar modules, petrochemicals, steel, textiles, health-related goods, construction materials and automotive products. The report pointed out that India's solar module capacity is nearly three times its domestic demand, while stressing that industrial investment and production capacity should also be assessed against domestic consumption, export markets and future demand. GTRI further argued that the proposed tariff relief does not require countries to undertake any actual changes in their industrial capacity, which it said undermines the stated rationale of the investigation. "Tariff relief without reform" is the central concern highlighted in the report, which warns that countries could secure lower duties simply by granting unilateral trade concessions even if the industrial conditions prompting the investigation remain unchanged. Warning that the threat of Graham tariffs of up to 100 per cent continues to hang over India, GTRI called on New Delhi to resist pressure to enter into what it described as an unequal trade arrangement. The report recommended that India address the US allegations sector by sector and demonstrate that its industrial investments cater to domestic buyers, overseas customers and future demand. GTRI said India should defend its industrial expansion on economic grounds rather than allow export growth alone to be treated as evidence of excess capacity.
news.summary: GTRI said Trump’s proposed tariffs revive a reciprocal regime under a new name, with a dual-rate structure to pressure countries into trade deals

news.title: Be Thankful Our Enemies Are Clowns
news.text:
Don’t go into Thanksgiving Day grumbling and black-pilled. Go in cheerful, excited, and most of all, thankful. Yeah, thankful. I know we got creamed at the midterms and that a bunch of communists are taking over not only Capitol Hill but some of our most beloved free states. I know that Iran is still Iran, and that affordability has not yet returned. I know that your retirement accounts took a beating that was only mildly mitigated by the Nvidia board forgiving the misuse of Jensen’s Huang.

But advocating for being thankful is not the result of some Pollyannaish delusion. Refusing to give in when faced with hardship is the only valid life strategy. It’s the only one that brings success. Be thankful for what you’ve got and then get to work getting more. Be especially thankful that our enemies are even dumber than our allies.

I never understood pessimists. That’s not because I think everything’s going to work out great. I’ve written a dozen novels – get my latest, "American Warlord" – about how things go completely to hell, so it’s not as if I’m someone who turns away from bad things. I try to be objective. I try to see things as they are. I fight on the battlefield they drop me on. Being a pessimist just seems like the easy way out. No one ever won by taking the easy way out.

Yeah, things can look down, but things turn around. Everything’s a cycle. You know, like the dirty hippies used to sing, turn, turn, turn. Right now we are in mourning for the destruction of our congressional majorities, not that they did much in the last year, but we would prefer to have them rather than not have them. And there are a lot of people are dooming about how it’s going to be years before we even have a chance to come back. But jump into your handy-dandy time machine – OK, it’s going to be a little while before AI makes time machines, but you know that’s coming – and go back two years. You were hearing the same sort of stuff. You were hearing the same sort of negativity. It’s just that it was the Democrats assuring themselves that they were royally screwed. And two years later, here we are. We’ve done the political Parent Trap.

I don’t want to minimize the problems we’ll face. We’ll face a lot of them, and there are risks. Gooey Republicans might find common cause with Democrats for shoving some version of amnesty down our throats. President Trump might not be able to end this Iran war with an unequivocal victory. The economy could flounder – the Democrats certainly want it to and will do everything they can to screw us over. But it doesn’t make sense to take counsel of your fears. Never prepare for failure. Fight for success and prepare to seize more success thereafter.

Conservatives tend to have a dim view of humanity, since they aren’t delusional leftists full of utopian nonsense. It’s not unusual for cons to find the cloud behind the silver lining. For a long time, before Ronald Reagan came along, conservatives never seemed to be happy. But Ronald Reagan was happy. He was an optimist. He was the Shining City on the Hill guy. And it was not, as his critics insisted, because he was dumb. He wasn’t dumb. He was a smart, serious guy who understood the criticality of morale. Like Napoleon, who famously said (and I am paraphrasing here) that 75 percent of success in battle is morale, he understood that you’re never going to win if you don’t think you can win. When you don’t think you can win, you stop trying to win. You just prepare yourself for the next loss. And then – surprise – that loss you anticipated comes to fruition.

The power of positive thinking is real. How many teams have you seen go out on the field muttering how they suck and they’re going to lose, then walk back off victorious? Not many.

The fact is that we have options and opportunities. What we have to do is be thankful for them and use them wisely. Remember, when you are suffering a setback in battle, your job is to rally, retake the initiative, and counterattack. Well, we lost one hell of a battle in the midterms. Now we’ve got to rally, retake the initiative, and counterattack.

Yes, I know that some of our forces are weak and lame. But enough about Sen. John Thune (R-SD). We got some outstanding senators and congressmen out there who can take the fight to the enemy. We’ve also lost a bunch of the garbage losers who’ve been holding us back. It’s a smaller caucus, to be sure, but there are fewer per capita GOP jackasses to get in the way. And that’s not all. We’ve got a Supreme Court that believes in our Constitution. Obviously, we’ve got the White House and therefore the executive branch. Plus, we’ve got top-notch contenders for 2028. We should be thankful for all that. And we should be thinking about how best to exploit these advantages.

We should be especially thankful for our enemies. This is a big one. This is crucial. The Democrats may have stumbled into success in the midterms with polling favorability on par with herpes, but they are a disaster. It was pure dumb luck – they were lucky the GOP was so dumb. These are not genius-level Bond villains stroking their cats in their volcano lairs. This pathetic party is a stunning collection of pinko mediocrities who won not because of what they are saying, but because they weren’t Republicans. Yep, they’ve got a big majority in the House, most of them having taken Republican seats by just a few votes. This makes these stolen seats prime candidates for recovery next time. Sure, they could play it smart and promote a moderate, common-sense agenda that pushes legislation that will provide real relief to real people. Or they could do exactly what Democrats do and spend all their time futilely trying to impeach Donald Trump, trying to raise taxes on productive people, and trying to outlaw cisgenderism.

Donald Trump has the opportunity to position himself as the voice of reason opposing the inevitable excesses of the ideologically unmoored Democrats. He can also position himself as Mr. Economy and spend this time talking about new factories, new regulatory cuts, and new opportunities, instead of that stupid reflecting pool. No one cares about the damn reflecting pool right now, although we should all be thankful that his work in Washington has started to make it a capital we can be proud of again.

I was struck by the positive outlook of the folks on the Salem/Townhall Gulf of America cruise last week. I was thinking it was going to be a Viking death ship complete with funeral pyre for our ruined conservative dreams. But no. People understood we got beat, but they were looking for the next fight, and therefore the next victory. No black-pilling. No dooming. No whining.

I’m not proposing you be satisfied with what we’ve got. We can always get more in terms of freedom, security, and prosperity for our country. But what we have isn’t nothing. What we have is not by chance. It’s by the hard work of millions of Americans over hundreds of years, as well as the favor of divine Providence. Yeah, we have problems, but we are Americans, and we’re not going to be defeated by the kind of losers who oppose us. That’s something we should be thankful for every single day.

news.title: Thanksgrifting
news.text:
The losers who don’t know how to give thanks.

Mossad folks tend to keep their mouths shut — that’s part of their business. My wife’s cousin used to point out where their office is while saying that it was forbidden to point out where their office was. So it was a bit of a surprise when former Mossad chief David Barnea casually mentioned that it was his outfit that prevented an ISIS attack at a Taylor Swift concert in Vienna. According to his explanation, the Austrians provided raw intelligence which the Mossad “processed” and helped to bring an end to the plot and the arrest of the terrorists. This is a beautiful example of how things are supposed to work. Unfortunately, Israel is one big one-way street, both when I drive around here and in the world at large.

After the announcement that Israel helped prevent a repeat of the Manchester Arena bombing, I would have expected Taylor Swift to put out a statement thanking the Mossad for its efforts to keep her fans safe. And maybe she made a private call to Binyamin Netanyahu and offered five discs as her form of thanks. But thanks from lefties are rare. They feel totally entitled, and anything done for them was deserved, earned, and expected. Swift is wealthy, talented, and also smart. She knows that if she were to thank Israel, she would anger her mostly lefty fan base. What is it worth saying thanks if the paying customers will stop buying her music and merchandise? Remember when she threw her support to Kamala Harris? How did a reelected Donald Trump repay her? He congratulated her on the announcement of her engagement to football star Travis Kelce. Trump is in another league compared to the ingrates on the left.

Thanksgiving was always beloved — lots of family, food, and football. A long weekend and then...shopping. I was in the open market “shuk” recently and saw a big turkey at one of the local butchers. It was waiting for its American patron to buy it. “Jews” are called in Hebrew, “Yehudim”, from the name of the fourth son of Jacob, Yehuda. The root of this name is “Hoda’a” which means thanks. Not far from my house is Rechov (street in Hebrew) George Washington. At the end of it, you will find Rechov Abraham Lincoln. Not far outside of Jerusalem, one can find a quiet, pastoral place in the John F. Kennedy Forest. The first street one hits when arriving in Tel Aviv has always been Laguardia. There are three 9/11 memorials in Israel — and not because of the Israelis or even the Jews who were killed on that day. It is a testament to the bond that Israel feels for America and the American people. A friend of mine who was no great fan of Donald Trump had only praise when the president returned to the White House and began sending war material that had been held up by the Biden administration.

Giving thanks at a minimum requires a person to peer outside of himself. If one believes that he either deserves or has earned everything, then why should he say, “thank you”? If someone paid a lot of money for a flight, why should he thank the flight attendant who brings his dinner? On the one hand, he paid for the meal as part of the price of his ticket. On the other hand, he can show some appreciation towards another human being who did his or her best to make life just a little bit more pleasant. She could throw the food tray at him, or they could announce that people can pick up the food on their own. One thing you almost never see from the left or their Muslim friends is gratitude. It’s always complaints, accusations, and demands. They are the most miserable people enjoying the highest standard of living ever created on this planet. It’s a farce to see some anti-fossil fuel ninny or Jew-hating ogre using an iPhone. Israel probably has some tech in it, and coal/oil were used in its manufacture and transport to market. These people are deranged narcissists and can’t see beyond the end of their noses.

While I am glad that a potential attack in Austria was averted, one has to call a time-out and really think about this arrangement. Ireland is competing with Spain and France to be the most antisemitic, Israel-hating country in Europe. Their “leaders” ran to recognize a nonexistent country, “Palestine,” as a reward for Hamas’ murder of 1,200 Israelis. They never stop accusing Israel of genocide and starving the fat Gazan population. They even wanted to remove the name of a former Israeli president and son of the Emerald Isle — and father of the current Israeli president — from a Dublin Park. But, lo and behold, despite a threatened boycott of Israeli tech, Irish police bought an Israeli anti-drone system. My feeling is that there comes a time to stop helping one’s enemies.

Israel famously removed a brain tumor from Yahya Sinwar, so that he could turn around and orchestrate the mass murder of Jews on October 7, 2023. At what point does Israel identify friends like the US, help them, and remember enemies and tell them to pound sand? Does Israel somehow have a moral obligation to help its enemies? Let’s say that it uncovers a plot through signal intelligence of a plan to blow up a major tower in Riyadh. Does Israel have to pass along this information to the Saudis via the US? Can’t they just buy a lot of popcorn and wait for it to happen? On the one hand, it was obviously good that the planned attack at the Swift concert did not occur. On the other hand, what has Austria done to reduce the anti-Israel hatred in Europe? Why is Israel always driving on one-way streets with unfriendly countries? Israel provides intelligence, tech, and sometimes manpower — like in earthquakes. And all she receives in return are complaints, threats, and boycotts.

One of the more difficult aspects of World War II involved the work at Bletchley Park. There were many plans and attacks that the code-breakers there discovered prior to their occurrence. When the British could send a plane or ship to “accidentally” discover the plans, they would. But there were cases where, under the orders of Winston Churchill, Allied soldiers and sailors died in order to prevent the Germans from knowing that their codes had been broken. I am sure that these were not easy decisions — to sacrifice men and equipment so that they could continue to decipher messages. Estimates say that the work on the Enigma and other coding machines may have reduced the length of the war by a year or two.

So should Israel send Spain anti-terror tech or critical intelligence? What is the difference between sending some high-tech military gear to France or Iran? Why does Israel provide intelligence to countries like England that blackball its native companies? Will Israel ever get over its battered wife syndrome and start telling its former friends and partners to go pound sand or show public gratitude? Send them flowers before the funerals, and maybe they will come to their senses: choose between the left/Muslim death spiral or work with Israel to be safe and prosperous.

Israel apparently warned the Trump administration of Iranian plans to harm top administration officials. This is the way it should work: Israel is grateful and helps its big friend. I don’t know if it needs to be so forthcoming to losers and ingrates like the leaders of Europe. Churchill didn’t enjoy hiding England’s knowledge, but he did it for a greater good. Israel might wish to learn from him. Reward your friends and let your enemies fend for themselves.
