news.title: Pete Hegseth, Pentagon Officials Discussed Using Wartime Law To Pressure Nvidia Board Over Jensen Huang's Return: Report
news.text: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and other senior Pentagon officials discussed using the Defense Production Act as leverage to pressure Nvidia's board to reinstate chief executive Jensen Huang. Hegseth and his senior deputy, Steve Feinberg, raised the 1950 law during weekend deliberations among senior Trump administration officials. Nvidia's board formally restored Huang as CEO on Monday morning.The Wall Street Journal reports to growing scrutiny of the administration's role in Huang's return. The editorial board wrote on Monday that President Donald Trump's "extraordinary political intervention will have legal and political costs." The Journal argued that the US economy should not hinge on one man and one company, and suggested that Trump assured the board his administration would not punish the company over possible export-control or securities violations if it rehired Huang.Jensen Huang Once Washed Dishes At Denny’s; Restaurant Now Restores Plaque At Booth Where Nvidia Was BornAccording to the report, Pentagon leaders argued that Huang's leadership was vital to US national security. The two officials discussed how the Defense Production Act could be used as leverage to push the board to restore an executive at a company they described as critical to national security. One person familiar with the talks described the mechanism - the act could be used to force Nvidia to shift more of its production to military projects. Another account of the discussions said officials explored diverting a greater share of manufacturing capacity to military work unless the board brought Huang back. The Post noted that such a move could cut into Nvidia's production plans and profits.Pentagon denies the accountA Pentagon official, speaking anonymously, rejected the report. The official said the conversations described between senior Defense Department leaders never happened and that no such proposal was made by the Secretary, the Deputy Secretary or the Under Secretary. The Post's report, as relayed by other outlets, also left open how far the idea travelled. It was unclear whether the proposal reached Trump or Vice President JD Vance, and a person familiar with the board's thinking said the board did not view the talks as a threat.Jensen Huang Bets On AI Agents, But Anthropic Tests How Rogue They Can Get If There’s A ChanceWhat the law allowsThe Defense Production Act gives the president wide latitude to direct domestic manufacturing capacity toward national defense needs, but does not explicitly authorise the government to appoint or reinstate corporate executives. Bill Greenwalt of the conservative American Enterprise Institute told the Post that the law does not support tying up Nvidia in government contracts, and that export controls would be a more effective tool.White House pushThe reported Pentagon discussions took place alongside a broader administration effort. Trump and Vance became convinced Huang had to return and were willing to use federal muscle in a Cabinet 'full-court press' over the weekend. Trump told CNBC he spoke to Nvidia's board directly about reinstating Huang. Vance worked to assure the board that the administration did not believe Huang had committed a crime or posed a national security risk.Nvidia's own statement on Monday said the board received input from senior levels of the U.S. government and, based on that input, is confident Huang's reinstatement poses no national security risk.Reaction in WashingtonElizabeth Warren, the incoming chair of the Senate Banking Committee, called the decision to reinstate Huang "reckless" and said executives and the board "still owe Congress answers." Democratic Senator Kirsten Gillibrand demanded public testimony from both Huang and the board. Huang is due to testify before the Senate Banking Committee in December.BackgroundHuang resigned on November 12 after reports that he had extramarital affairs. The board said days later that it did not plan to bring him back, then voted unanimously on November 23 to reinstate him. news.title: Moment FedEx plane overshoots the runway at notorious Miami airport forcing emergency ground stop on Thanksgiving Eve leaving travelers stranded
news.text:
A FedEx cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) to issue a ground stop as travelers raced to get home for Thanksgiving.

The FedEx McDonnell Douglas MD-11 cargo plane originating from Frederick W Smith International Airport in Memphis, Tennessee, veered off the runway at around 8.40pm, with photos and video shared online showing the aircraft sitting in the grass. Emergency crews were then seen surrounding the aircraft.

No injuries were reported, but the runway incursion has shut down all but one of the runways at the international airport – leading the FAA to halt all incoming air traffic.

According to an FAA advisory, departures bound for Miami were grounded starting at 8.16pm and remained in effect until at least 9.35pm, though there is between a 30 percent and 60 percent chance that the ground stop will be extended.

The incident marks the second time this year that a cargo plane overshot the runway in Miami, after an Amazon plane crashed and killed five people in September.

Earlier this month, a UPS flight also collided with a Copa Airlines flight while taxiing at Miami International Airport.

Travelers flying into or out of Miami International Airport are now urged to check directly with their airlines for potential delays.

It now remains unclear what may have caused the runway incursion, though it was raining at the time the plane landed.

The FAA is now investigating the incident, and said on social media at 9.41pm ET that flights were expected to resume shortly. 

But as of 10.18pm ET, 41 percent of outgoing flights from Miami were delayed as were 28 percent of incoming flights, according to FlightAware.

In total, there were 6,120 flights delayed across the United States on Wednesday with 77 total cancelations as 81 million people were expected to travel, according to AAA. 

Travelers have already experienced flight chaos, when an 'equipment outage' caused a ground stop at Chicago O'Hare International Airport and Delta Air Lines experienced an outage.

On Tuesday, the FAA issued a ground stop at Chicago's O'Hare Airport at 4.06pm ET, holding all aircraft at their departure gates.

The ground stop was then lifted shortly after 5pm, when the FAA issued a ground delay, which was expected to remain until Wednesday morning.

The FAA cited a ⁠technical issue with a ​ground surveillance radar and ​tracking system for Tuesday's disruptions.

The system is used by air traffic control to ​monitor aircraft and ​vehicles on airport runways and taxiways.

Just a few days earlier, on Sunday, more than 3,500 flights were delayed at airports across the country on Sunday morning because of an outage affecting Delta Air Lines.

The FAA issued a ground stop for all flights heading to Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport because of an issue with Delta's automated system for departing flight weight and balance calculations. 

But the domino effect also stalled take-off's elsewhere as crews struggled to turn planes around for their following departures.

United Airlines flights across the United States were also grounded last week, when the airline announced on social media that it was experiencing a 'widespread system outage' as it apologized to customers 'for the inconvenience.'

Earlier this month, a technical issue prompted the FAA to ground all flights nationwide. 

The Air Traffic Control System Command Center has since explained that the halting of 3,500 US flights for five hours was 'due to extraordinary circumstances for safety reasons'. 

'There has been a temporary telecommunications outage - out of an abundance of caution, all flights have been halted,' the FAA said. 

'Every flight has been accounted for, and international flights will be handled on a case-by-case basis.'

President Donald Trump has since blamed half-century-old aviation equipment for the ground stop, which led to thousands of cancellations and travel woes for over a million passengers. 

'We have old, broken equipment,' the president said last week, noting that some of the equipment that went down was 55 years old.

'We essentially want to blow it up and put new in, and we can do it simultaneously with very little trouble. What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack,' he said.
news.summary: A FedEx cargo plane overshot the runway at Miami International Airport on Wednesday, prompting the Federal Aviation Administration to issue a ground stop.

news.title: How US States Are Bracing for Powerful Thanksgiving Storms, Flooding
news.text: As severe weather interrupts Thanksgiving travel and brings heavy rain, snow and flooding to parts of the U.S. this week, local leaders around the country are preparing emergency resources to mitigate the damage. On the West Coast, California Governor Gavin Newsom declared a statewide emergency in September in anticipation of what experts are calling a "Super El Niño." On Wednesday, parts of the state were already seeing record-high tides and flooding. Evacuation warnings and orders had been issued for Santa Barbara, Santa Cruz, Ventura, and Humboldt counties. In an email to Newsweek Wednesday, a spokesperson for the California Governor's Office of Emergency Services said the state had been taking proactive steps in preparation for the storm this week. "California is not waiting for disaster to strike before taking action," said the spokesperson. "As we enter the holiday weekend and continue through this El Niño season, our priority remains the safety of all Californians.” In a statement issued Tuesday, Newsom said the state had distributed containers full of sanbags and other flood-fighting supplies across the state. The governor said emergency crews, the National Guard and medical support were also on standby. Preparations in Other States On the East Coast, the leaders of New Jersey and New York also declared a State of Emergency. New York Governor Kathy Hochul declared an emergency for Long Island, New York City, Westchester and contiguous counties ahead of a severe storm expected to bring damaging winds and heavy rainfall to New York, possibly causing power outages and travel disruptions. Other states also at risk of outages include Oregon, Montana, Maryland, Virginia, West Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Tennessee, Vermont, Rhode Island, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New Jersey, New York, Pennsylvania, Georgia, California, Washington, Delaware, and Missouri. "As New Yorkers gather with their friends and family this Thanksgiving, my message is simple: Do not take the impact of this strong coastal storm lightly,” said Hochul. "I've directed state resources to ensure we are equipped to take on this storm, keep power on and stand ready to respond." New Jersey Governor Mikie Sherrill also declared a state of emergency Wednesday, urging residents to be prepared for prolonged power outages and road closures. "Please travel today if possible, charge your devices, and never drive through flooded roadways," Sherrill said on X. Florida is also experiencing heavy rainfall and severe flooding, with hundreds of emergency response workers mobilizing to help residents. President Donald Trump approved a major disaster declaration to help the state recover from flooding that started in October. The National Weather Service said a coastal low-pressure system was expected to bring heavy rain, severe storms and flooding to South Florida ahead of Thanksgiving, while east-central and northeastern Florida continue to deal with historic river and flooding from earlier this fall. "In response to severe flooding, the State of Florida has been focused on saving lives, supporting residents in need, and keeping critical services available,” said Governor Ron DeSantis on X. “State personnel have completed nearly 500 floodwater rescues, and more than 10,000 feet of Tiger Dams have been deployed to protect critical infrastructure."
news.summary: States across the U.S. are preparing for severe weather around the Thanksgiving holiday.

news.title: The devastating scale of Putin’s war on Ukraine laid bare as leaked figures show 500,000 Russian soldiers dead
news.text:
Nearly 500,000 Russian soldiers have been killed in almost five years of war with Ukraine, according to confidential government figures leaked this week.

Data from the state statistics agency Rosstat shows that at least 490,334 Russian soldiers have been killed in the conflict since February 2022, according to analysis by the BBC.

The figures show how the invasion became the leading cause of death for 18-24 year olds in Russia, with 65% of those who died last year killed in the conflict.

It also sheds light on the monumental losses sustained to make limited advances into Ukraine, with some 20,000 soldiers dying for control of 10 villages with a total pre-war population under 12,000.

Ukraine reported this summer that 50,000 personnel had been killed since the 2022 invasion, a tenth of the figure recorded by Rosstat.

And the Ukrainian military estimates that Russia has now taken more than 1,643,000 casualties, including dead and wounded - more than three times the figure last reported by Kyiv.

A corpus of 11 million death certificates collected from February 2022 to September 2026 suggests that casualty rates have steadily increased for Russia over the duration of the war.

The information was initially obtained by the hacking groups Cyber Partisans and Silent Crow, who claimed to have obtained mortality data within dozens of terabytes of information from Rosstat.

The upward casualty rate seems to have peaked at 5,352 deaths per week in March of last year, although the BBC notes delays in the reporting of deaths thereafter and incomplete data for 2026.

Russia currently occupies the majority of a fortified eastern region known as the Donbas, but has struggled to expand its control of Ukraine.

Around 325,000 troops may have been killed in the fiercely contested Donetsk region alone, according to a separate analysis by independent Russian outlet Agentstvo.

The Rosstat leak also suggests that more than 1,000 Russian soldiers have taken their own lives since the invasion of Ukraine, according to further analysis by The Guardian.

The figures rise significantly when including soldiers reported missing; analysis by exiled Russian outlets Meduza and Mediazona tallied 490,000 losses up to September 2026, rising past 700,000 when accounting for those missing in action.

Ukraine, like Russia, does not publicly report on its own casualties, citing operational secrecy. But Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky said late in July that Kyiv had suffered around 450,000 casualties, including 50,000 deaths and 400,000 wounded.

Both sides have given wildly different estimates of each others’ casualties with no way to independently verify the data.

British intelligence estimated in September that around 500,000 Russian soldiers had been killed since the start of the invasion, in line with the BBC analysis of Rosstat’s estimates.

The anonymous UA Losses website meanwhile estimates that some 115,952 Ukrainian troops have been killed since 2022.

Ukraine’s general staff reported on November 25 that Russia had taken 2,091 casualties in the past day alone, reflecting a steady upward trend since 2022.

By comparison, Moscow was taking a mean average 415 casualties each day in October 2022; 709 in October 2023; 1,354 in October 2024; and 1,008 in October 2025, based on estimates from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

Ukraine assessed in September that Russia had taken 300,000 casualties so far this year - 18% of the casualties in 16% of the time since the invasion. On Tuesday, 24 November, the figure had risen to 432,519 casualties.

Western officials believe the toll is becoming unmanageable for Russia and in August estimated that the Kremlin was losing six thousand more troops per month than it was able to enlist.

The trend has only worsened, with October 2026 becoming the deadliest month for Russian combat losses since 2022, according to Ukraine’s general staff.

The American CSIS estimated in January that Russia was then taking casualties at a ratio of around 2:1, or “2.5:1”. Modern militaries hold as a rule of thumb that an attacking ground force should outnumber defenders by around 3:1 to have a good chance of overwhelming a prepared opponent.

Putin can still draw on a much larger population to prosecute his war, even five years in. In September, he authorised another expansion of the military - the fourth this year - allowing Moscow to stand 2,441,630 units, including 1,550,500 active duty military personnel. Up to 640,000 Russian troops are currently deployed against Ukraine, the European Parliament estimated in February.

Ukraine had a comparative force of around 677,000 active duty personnel available last year, up from 209,000 in 2021, although estimates vary.

The growing exchanges this year has seen a “dramatically” higher toll of civilian casualties in Ukraine than in any year since the full-scale invasion in 2022, according to the UN.

New data shows that in October 2026, the number of civilians killed (372) and injured (1981) - was 95 per cent higher than in October last year, according to the UN Human Rights Monitoring Mission in Ukraine (HRMMU).

Almost 18,000 civilians have been killed and almost 58,000 have been injured in Ukraine alone since the invasion, the UN said. And the figure continues to climb as Russia ramps up its attacks on areas housing civilians.

On November 2, a school in Komyshuvakha, southeastern Ukraine, was hit by several bombs, killing at least 72 people and leaving four missing, according to local authorities.

The UNHCR said Russian long-range drone and missile strikes remain the leading cause of all civilian casualties in Ukraine, accounting for 55 per cent of the tally for October. Moscow has denied deliberately targeting civilian targets in Ukraine.

There is no comprehensive, verified figure for the number of Russian civilians killed during the war in Ukraine. But Russia’s permanent representative to the UN, Vassily Nebenzia, claimed this month that Ukrainian attacks had caused “about 37,000 civilian casualties” including 9,200 deaths and nearly 28,000 injured between February 2022 and late September 2026.

“The third quarter of 2026 was particularly bloody,” he acknowledged. “Almost 102,000 munitions were recorded to have been fired at civilian facilities in Russia, an increase of 85 per cent compared to the previous period.”

Between July and September, Nebenzia said, 631 people were killed and another 4,400 were injured, averaging 54 casualties every day. 

Nebenzia did not provide evidence for his claims and it was unclear whether he was referring to Russian territory or territory in occupied Ukraine. Ukraine also denies deliberately targeting civilian targets.

Russia and Ukraine last month finally agreed to a humanitarian ceasefire to evacuate the devastated Ukrainian town of Oleshky, where some 6,000 residents had been trapped without regular access to food, water or electricity. Many were said to have resorted to cooking garden weeds and pigeons to survive. 

Talks aimed at ending the conflict restarted in Abu Dhabi this month but diplomats came away without a clear breakthrough.

Russian forces have been subjecting Kyiv and other Ukrainian cities to near-constant attacks since September, hoping continued pressure will hand them leverage in future talks.

But Ukraine has pushed back in recent weeks with debilitating attacks on the bridge connecting Russia to occupied Crimea and wider strikes on targets in Libya and the Gulf of Finland.

Kyiv has also piled pressure on to Moscow to end the war with growing strikes on energy infrastructure and big businesses in Russia, squeezing the economy behind its war machine.

But Zelensky says Ukraine will still need to find a further $25bn in external support just to keep it in the fight next year.

And Russia appears to retain its maximalist demands of Ukraine, urging Kyiv to give up huge swathes of its territory in exchange for peace as US president Donald Trump accuses Zelensky of prolonging the war.
news.summary: Vladimir Putin still demands huge concessions from Ukraine, but leaked data from his main stats agency suggests the losses are only getting worse with time, writes James C. Reynolds
news.author: James C. Reynolds

news.title: Judge Blocks FCC Review of ABC Licenses as Commissioner Praises Ruling
news.text: A federal judge on Wednesday night ruled to temporarily block the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from reviewing ABC's broadcast licenses early, saying in part, "This is not a close case. Plaintiffs have a weighty interest in 'vindicating the[ir] right to be free of retaliation for [their] protected speech.'” The judge's ruling landed the backing of the commission's only Democrat, Anna Gomez. Taking to X Wednesday night, Commissioner Gomez said, "This decision shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights." In a separate post, Gomez added, "Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I've said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side." Newsweek reached out to the FCC, Disney and the White House via email Wednesday night for comment. What To Know The FCC's leadership is comprised of Chairman Brendan Carr, Commissioner Olivia Trusty and Commissioner Gomez. Trusty was nominated by President Donald Trump, as was Carr. The chairman was also renominated by former President Joe Biden in 2023, as was Gomez. Last month, ABC asked U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan to halt the review of the licenses held by television stations owned by the company. In Wednesday's ruling, AliKhan, a Biden appointee, OK'd ABC’s request in part for a preliminary injunction and temporary restraining order. "Accordingly, the court determines that Plaintiffs have met their burden of showing causation at this stage. They are thus likely to succeed on their First Amendment claim," the federal judge wrote in part on Wednesday. Gomez has previously accused the FCC of carrying out a “sustained, coordinated campaign of censorship and control” against Disney and warned that the early license reviews for ABC represented what she called the agency’s most serious "assault on the First Amendment" to date. The dispute originates from Carr's directive earlier this year ordering the stations to undergo early license reviews even though their renewals were not scheduled to begin until at least 2028. The order was one day after Trump called for late-night host Jimmy Kimmel to be fired. In Wednesday's ruling, AliKhan wrote in part, "Turning to temporal proximity, against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings." The judge also said that "Chairman Carr has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders." The FCC has linked its move to its investigation into Disney’s diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) practices, while Disney and ABC argue that the reviews are part of an effort to retaliate against the network over programming criticized by the president. Disney sued the FCC in August. Dave Aronberg, former Palm Beach County State Attorney, told Newsweek that AliKhan made the right call. "The FCC can regulate broadcasters, but a broadcast license doesn’t come with a White House veto over what goes on the air." Aronberg added, "The FCC ordered early reviews of eight ABC station licenses the day after President Trump called for Jimmy Kimmel to be fired. That creates a chilling effect on free speech and a likely First Amendment violation. Even if a station never loses its license, the threat may have already done its job." In a statement to The Hill regarding the ruling, an FCC spokesperson said that the preliminary injunction is "wrong on the facts and wrong on the law—as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear.” “The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter,” the spokesperson told the outlet. "We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.” Seth Stern, Freedom of the Press Foundation's chief of advocacy, said in a released statement sent to Newsweek Wednesday night that "The judge saw the FCC’s attempts to punish ABC for what they are: a campaign of intimidation and retaliation against speech that displeases Donald Trump. The First Amendment does not allow government officials to appoint themselves the journalism or comedy police. The Constitution recognizes that even good-faith government actors cannot adjudicate journalistic merits without letting political agendas cloud their judgment, and Brendan Carr is far from a good-faith actor." Stern added that ABC is not alone in what he labeled "the FCC’s censorship spree." "Outlets that Carr has intimidated can breathe a little easier. The lesson to learn from this ruling is don’t cave to Carr or any other anti-speech bullies in this administration. Instead, take them to court — the judiciary is on to them, and they lose regularly," Stern concluded. Read The Order in Full Newsweek’s reporters and editors used Martyn, our AI assistant, to produce this story. Learn more about Martyn here. Contact Newsweek editors on this story: Edward T. Cummins
news.summary: The judge's ruling Wednesday night landed the backing of the commission's only Democrat, Anna Gomez.
news.author: Anna Commander

news.title: Trump and NATO chief urge Russia to avoid actions that widen Ukraine war
news.text:
WASHINGTON: Russia should avoid actions that expand its war in Ukraine, US President Donald Trump and NATO chief Mark Rutte said in a joint statement on Wednesday (Nov 26) after a meeting in Florida where they also discussed the Iran war.

The meeting came after the Republican leader, who has been critical of America's Western ⁠allies, met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese leader Xi Jinping last week in Asia, referring to each as his "friend."

"We also discussed the importance of Russia avoiding any actions that intentionally, or unintentionally, expand the war, and the importance of obtaining a peaceful resolution to the war as rapidly as possible," the leaders said in their statement.

Trump's meeting with ​Putin triggered a backlash from domestic Democratic opponents and European allies, with the latter having ‌pushed ⁠to be included in US-backed talks to end the war in Ukraine.

Rutte, who has repeatedly tried to soothe tension within NATO ​and keep Trump onside, has said it was normal for major ​nuclear powers to meet.

Rutte and Trump also talked about boosting defence spending and investment in the United States and across NATO, according to their statement.

The war in Ukraine and US-Israeli war on Iran were the primary subjects of the talks, it added, but did not say what was discussed on Iran.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, who has ​been criticised by Trump, has said Europe had to be included in peace ​talks.

Trump has often criticised Washington's Western and democratic allies over issues such as NATO spending, trade tariffs and what he calls their inadequate support for the war on Iran.

news.title: Denny's Rehangs Jensen Huang's Plaque, Tells Him 'Your Booth Is Waiting'
news.text: Denny's has a message for Jensen Huang, two days after Nvidia's board voted to bring him back: "Jensen, your booth is waiting and the coffee's on." The diner chain's post on X on Wednesday also disclosed that the plaque marking the San Jose booth associated with Nvidia's founding came down during Huang's brief departure from the company. Denny's said it learned of the removal on Friday, November 13, the day after Nvidia announced his resignation, and "put the plaque right back up where it belongs." It did not say who took it down, or why. The statement, which had drawn more than 2 million views by Wednesday evening, also showed that Denny's reached out to Nvidia while the scandal was still unfolding. "On the morning of November 10, we wrote to NVIDIA's communications team: 'Jensen is part of our history, and we are part of his,'" the chain wrote. That was two days after Huang admitted in a letter to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife, and two days before he resigned. Newsweek asked Denny's who removed the plaque, why it was removed and whether its removal was authorized by the company. A Founding Story Under Pressure The booth is one of the best-known origin stories in American business, and Huang has long embraced his Denny's roots, returning in 2023 to recall the shifts he worked there as a teenager before founding the company at the center of the AI boom. Denny's is now claiming that history publicly, even as Huang's return remains under scrutiny in Washington over his relationship with a woman the House Intelligence Committee has called a "publicly reported Chinese intelligence asset," an allegation China's Foreign Ministry called "entirely groundless." From the Dish Pit to a Trillion-Dollar Booth In 1993, Huang, Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem met at the Denny's in San Jose to sketch out a chip that could bring realistic 3D graphics to personal computers, according to Nvidia. Thirty years later, on September 26, 2023, Huang returned for a ceremony with Denny's then-chief executive, Kelli Valade, to unveil the plaque. Huang, who got his first Denny's job in Portland, Oregon, at 15, told the crowd that day: "I was a dishwasher, I was a busboy, I waited tables." He added, "Denny's has taught me so many lessons." Huang's departure followed a tumultuous week in which he admitted in a letter to employees that he had been unfaithful to his wife. Reports have since linked him to Alice Huang, an executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed whom U.S. officials have scrutinized over possible ties to Chinese intelligence. The allegations are unproven, and Megaspeed has denied wrongdoing. On November 12, Nvidia announced that Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member, effective immediately, and named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress interim chief executive. Shares fell about 14 percent at the opening bell before closing down 4.3 percent. Huang's departure was short-lived. President Donald Trump wrote on Truth Social that bringing Huang back "would be the best thing for the company, and also, for the U.S.A." On Monday, Nvidia's board voted unanimously to reinstate him. "I can't wait to get back to work," Huang said. Denny's statement leans on the earlier chapter. "Think about all the people who've washed dishes in America's Diner over the years," it reads. "One of them went on to change the world, and he still remembers what he learned at the sink." The Coffee's On Denny's did not say who took the plaque down or why, only that it "learned" the plaque had come down and restored it. Huang's troubles in Washington are not over either. The House Intelligence Committee has requested a closed-door briefing with him, and Nvidia has said it will keep cooperating with government investigations. For now, Huang's plaque is back above the booth. Nvidia's official AI account replied to Denny's post with a single green heart.
news.summary: Denny's found Jensen Huang's plaque down the day after he resigned as Nvidia CEO. It put it back and says his booth is waiting.
news.author: Lars Hanson

news.title: Rupee falls 20 paise to 92.40 against US dollar in early trade

news.title: Hegseth pitched using wartime law to force Nvidia to reappoint Huang as CEO: Report
news.text:
US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth pushed for the use of the Defense Production Act (DPA), a Cold War-era wartime law, to force Nvidia to reappoint Jensen Huang as chief executive, according to The Washington Post.
The DPA grants the president the authority to mobilise private companies and redirect production on national security grounds. For example, the government can invoke the law to compel private firms to produce munitions, parachutes, spare parts for military equipment, and other essential supplies during wartime.
Hegseth and his allies at the Department of Defense wanted to use the DPA as a pressure tactic.
A source told The Post that Hegseth and his allies suggested the law could be deployed as a warning to Nvidia.
According to the source, the plan could have unfolded as follows: President Donald Trump would invoke the DPA to force Nvidia to shift more of its production towards military projects. Such a move could have reduced Nvidia's production targets and profits, making the company highly likely to comply with Trump's demands.
In the end, Trump intervened directly, and Nvidia's board reinstated Huang.
Earlier this month, Huang resigned after acknowledging that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a suspected Chinese spy. Alice is associated with Megaspeed, which remains under investigation for smuggling Nvidia chips into China.
Beyond the obvious concern that Alice may have used her relationship with Huang to smuggle Nvidia chips into China, there are fears that he may have divulged trade secrets or confidential internal policy deliberations within either Nvidia or the Trump administration.
There are also concerns that China may have influenced US policy on artificial intelligence and semiconductors through Alice's influence over Huang, who is highly influential on technology matters within the administration.
Trump, his allies, and Silicon Valley figures have rejected those national security concerns and backed Huang.
Hegseth aligns Defense Department with Silicon Valley
Hegseth's push to use the DPA echoed calls from Silicon Valley leaders to leverage the Department of Defense in support of Huang's reinstatement.
Cryptocurrency investor Balaji Srinivasan said last week that "there's actually a scenario where the Department of War steps in on Jensen's side".
"Why? Given the likely cyberattacks on Microsoft, flights, banks, and now NSA, it's arguably a matter of US national security to immediately return the most important person in AI to his role at the top AI company. Defense Production Act, but for the restoration of Jensen Huang," said Srinivasan.
As China hawks pushed for deeper investigations into Huang's conduct, Silicon Valley figures and the Maga movement rallied to his defence. They argued that Nvidia and Huang are critical to the American economy and should remain beyond reproach irrespective of any transgressions.
Several senior positions at the Department of Defense are occupied by figures with deep Silicon Valley ties. Billionaire Steve Feinberg serves as Deputy Secretary of Defense and Silicon Valley veteran Emil Michael serves as Under Secretary of Defense for Research and Engineering and Chief Technology Officer.
Together, they have aligned the Department of Defense more closely with the interests of Silicon Valley companies such as Anduril and Palantir, blurring the line between military-industrial cooperation and corporate influence. Critics argue that the industry is no longer merely influencing defence policy but increasingly shaping it from within the Department of Defense itself.

news.title: North Korea's Kim vows to build more nuclear weapons after ignoring Trump's overture
news.text:
APKim inspects nuclear facilities, vows to expand weapons arsenal amid Trump's outreach

Seoul: North Korean leader Kim Jong Un visited facilities that produce nuclear ingredients and called for building more nuclear weapons, days after ignoring US President Donald Trump's offer to meet during his recent visit to Asia.Kim's statement signals again that he won't give up his evolving nuclear program - the backbone of his authoritarian rule - and is eager to bolster his country's status as a nuclear power.The North's official Korean Central News Agency said Thursday that Kim inspected two nuclear materials production factories, one newly inaugurated and the other being expanded. KCNA photos showed Kim and senior military officials walking between dense rows of what appeared to be centrifuges used to produce weapons-grade uranium and touring halls displaying what were believed to be warheads. Some of the images were blurred.Also read: New Trump tariffs would likely increase sugar prices in the USKCNA said Kim visited a nuclear-powered equipment production base and a nuclear research institute as well on Wednesday.Live EventsNorth Korea has disclosed a uranium enrichment site a few times since it showed one at its main Yongbyon nuclear complex to visiting American scholars in 2010. North Korea didn't say where the nuclear materials production factories that Kim visited this week are located. In June, when North Korea disclosed parts of a uranium enrichment site while reporting on Kim's visit there, outside experts assessed it was likely an additional uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon.Kim justifies nuke program by citing threats from US, South KoreaKim said his latest inspection visit was part of efforts to strengthen North Korea's defence capabilities in response to "variable nuclear threats approaching the Korean Peninsula moment by moment," KCNA said.Also read: For Trump, doubling down on tariffs is about power, not popularityHe accused the US of inciting its regional allies to possess nuclear-powered submarines and committing to sharing its nuclear weapons with them, KCNA said."The validity and substantiality of our possession of nuclear weapons and the trend of bolstering up its nuclear capability in quality and quantity are an irreversible reality," Kim said, according to KCNA.Kim also said the deployment of low-yield battlefield nuclear weapons across multiple domains for various missions is crucial and urgent given North Korea's "inevitable reality facing the border with the most dangerous enemy state," a reference to South Korea. North Korea has in recent years focused on developing and deploying such tactical nuclear weapons amid heightened animosity with South Korea.South Korea's Defence Ministry said it takes Kim's comments on battlefield nuclear weapons seriously and added that Seoul maintains a firm military readiness against Pyongyang's nuclear threats under an alliance with the US.South Korea's Joint Chiefs of Staff declined to share an analysis of the North Korean nuclear facilities reported by KCNA, calling it confidential information for South Korea and the US.Kim has accelerated the expansion of his military nuclear program since his earlier high-stakes diplomacy with Trump collapsed in 2019. He has also shifted his foreign policy focus toward strengthening ties with Cold War-era allies Moscow and Beijing, seeking to strengthen his regional footing while pushing to establish North Korea as a permanent nuclear power.Trump still hopes to meet KimTrump reiterated his eagerness to restore diplomacy with Kim as he visited China last week for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit. But a Trump-Kim meeting didn't happen, with Pyongyang not publicly responding to Trump's overture.In an interview with the New York Post this week, Trump dismissed the suggestion that Kim had rebuffed his outreach, saying, "No, he didn't ignore it. You know, we had many leaders there ... There'll be a time when we meet ... It was just not really the right time. It was a very busy two-day period."Trump also claimed he could revive diplomacy with Kim at any time by restarting the exchange of letters they maintained during his first term, although he acknowledged that the two leaders had not corresponded "recently."Kim has previously said he could return to talks if the US drops its "hostile policy" against his country and respects what he calls the North's status as a nuclear state. Experts say Kim aims to win international recognition as a nuclear state so that he could demand the lifting of international sanctions.Last week, International Atomic Energy Agency Director General Rafael Grossi assessed North Korea has been expanding its original uranium enrichment facility at Yongbyon, calling the move "a cause for serious concern."Nuclear weapons can be built using either highly enriched uranium or weapons-grade plutonium, and North Korea has facilities to produce both at Yongbyon. Last year, South Korea's Unification Minister Chung Dong-young said that North Korea was operating four uranium enrichment facilities and that they were running every day. news.text: Days after U.S. President Donald Trump declared Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang not a security threat to the United States, a central question remains unanswered: Was the woman Huang was having an affair with a Chinese spy?Senior U.S. national security officials, including at the White House, FBI and the CIA, have debated that question in recent days in an effort to determine if Alice Huang — a former executive at a major Nvidia customer — was working for or passing information to China’s premier spy agency, according to five people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.The U.S. has collected intelligence on Alice Huang and her contact with individuals associated with China’s Ministry of State Security (MSS), said two of the people, who were briefed on the intelligence. news.title: Colombia drops its bid to join the BRICS bank in a new shift towards the United States
news.text:
Colombia drops its bid to join the BRICS bank in a new shift towards the United States

The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has abandoned Colombia's process of joining the New Development Bank, the financial arm of the BRICS group of emerging economies, which his predecessor Gustavo Petro began in 2025. The decision adds to other changes in Colombian foreign policy, now more closely aligned with the United States and Israel.

 The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has abandoned Colombia's process of joining the New Development Bank, the financial arm of the BRICS group of emerging economies, which his predecessor Gustavo Petro began in 2025. The decision adds to other changes in Colombian foreign policy, now more closely aligned with the United States and Israel.

In a statement released on Wednesday night, the Foreign Ministry headed by Omar Bula said Colombia “will not continue the actions aimed at securing such membership” of the group founded by Brazil, Russia, India, China and South Africa and of its bank. The text adds that the government will seek financing from “other multilateral organisations” for its 2026-2030 National Development Plan, but does not explain the reasons for the decision.

Petro applied to join the bank in Shanghai on May 16, 2025, shortly after bringing Colombia into China's Belt and Road Initiative. On June 19, the bank's president, former Brazilian President Dilma Rousseff, announced its approval, which the board of governors ratified in July. Because the bank's founding agreement is a treaty, ratification required a law from the Colombian Congress. The government submitted the bill on November 25, 2025, but it never came to a vote, and Colombia was listed as an observer in the process of joining.

Since taking office, De la Espriella has recognised Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights, opened Colombia's embassy in Jerusalem and withdrawn the country from the Hague Group, a coalition of countries critical of Israel's offensive in Gaza. According to the Colombian newspaper Portafolio, Donald Trump's nominee for ambassador in Bogotá, Nathaniel Morris, told the US Senate that De la Espriella had expressed his intention to take the country out of the Belt and Road Initiative, something the Colombian government has not confirmed.

The decision reflects the weight of the United States, which buys almost three in every ten dollars of Colombia's exports, according to the statistics agency DANE. China, however, has been the country's main supplier since 2021: between January and September, Colombia bought US$17.833 billion of goods from China, 26.7% more than a year earlier, against US$13.995 billion from the United States.
news.summary: The government of Colombian President Abelardo de la Espriella has abandoned Colombia's process of joining the New Development Bank, the financial arm of the BRICS group of emerging economies, which his predecessor Gustavo Petro began in 2025. The decision adds to other changes in Colombian foreign policy, now more closely aligned with the United States and Israel.

news.title: MARK RILEY: Misery index indicates Australians are facing worst hardships in 25 years
news.text:
There is a reason a lot of Australians feel miserable at the moment.

On the measure of a little-known economic indicator devised in the 1960s, they officially are.

That indicator is the Misery Index.

It calculates the level of everyday hardship by simply adding together the rate of inflation and the rate of unemployment.

According to leading economist Chris Richardson, the spike in inflation to 4.9 per cent on Wednesday — the same level as unemployment — meant that Australians are now more miserable than they have been in 25 years.

That combination lifted the average rate of misery under the Albanese Government to its highest level since the Howard era.

Back then it was persistent unemployment of about 6.5 per cent that pushed the index higher. Average inflation still hovered below the Reserve Bank’s 2 to 3 per cent range for most of the time, only really breaking out in 2000-2001 and in the 18 months before Kevin Rudd swept Howard from office in 2007.

The record for the Albanese Government has been quite different.

Its story has been one of persistently high inflation, outside the RBA’s target range.

A quick analysis of monthly inflation rates since the 2022 election reveals a pretty ordinary economic report card.

On day one, the official rate was 6.1 per cent and heading to its post-COVID high of 7.8 per cent in the December quarter of that year.

Since then, rates have only been below the 3 per cent ceiling of the target range for four of the Government’s 18 financial quarters in office.

And that record will extend to four of 19 quarters when the current December quarter figures become available.

The official consumer price index only fell below 3 per cent between September 2024 and June 2025.

It broke out above the range in September last year, five months before the first Israeli and US bombs fell on Tehran.

It has remained persistently above that level — and heading steadily higher — ever since.

No wonder people are feeling miserable.

Albanese and Treasurer Jim Chalmers point out justifiably that the principal drivers of inflation have been external.

The wars in Ukraine and Iran have sent international fuel prices through the roof.

And Donald Trump’s mercantilist tariffs haven’t helped either.

But it is the job of governments to build domestic buffers to these sorts of cyclical pressures. Those buffers are now proving inadequate.

The Albanese Government has taken understandable pride in rolling out big-spending Labor reforms that have improved the lot of working people.

But its social realignment agenda of cheaper medicines, cheaper child care, generous paid parental leave, fairer wages in the care sector and fee-free TAFE has come at enormous cost to taxpayers.

That is fine when revenues are booming. But when they’re not, it is a big problem.

The structural cost of those measures is now threatening to cripple the budget as it is pulverised by cyclical forces.

This Government has consistently boasted of the Australian economy’s “resilience”.

That had some resonance when unemployment was remaining steadfastly below 4 per cent.

Not anymore.

With both the inflation and jobless rates now threatening to break through 5 per cent, the domestic economy is no longer looking shock-proof.

People are feeling the pinch as we head into a Christmas period with a retail sector that is already buckling under heavy losses.

David Jones is at risk of going the way of the dodo and General Pants has lost its shirt.

Even Harvey Norman is struggling, despite every day in its stores looking like Black Friday with ticket prices cut by 30, 40 and 50 per cent.

Things are crook. The Government says they won’t remain that way forever. The cycle will turn. But it will take time.

Chalmers is sticking by Treasury’s prediction that inflation will fall back into the RBA’s target range in the second half of next year.

That’s despite the RBA pushing back its own prediction until the first half of 2028.

The wars in Iran and Ukraine will end. Eventually. But new wars or pandemics or trade or supply shocks could emerge.

One thing, though, is certain: the coming year will make or break the Albanese Government.

Its ability to regain the economic balance between spending and revenues at a time of unprecedented political dislocation will determine just how miserable or otherwise the Government will be at the 2028 election.

Mark Riley is the Seven Network’s political editor
news.summary: MARK RILEY: The last time Australians felt this miserable, John Howard was prime minister.
news.author: Mark Riley

news.title: Pensioners fear misery of January’s 'grotesque' energy bill hike
news.text: Scots pensioners have told of the misery January’s energy bill hike will heap on them. Households face a “staggering” 26% increase this winter after energy regulator Ofgem confirmed on Wednesday that the price cap – which limits how much power companies can charge customers on standard or default variable tariffs – will rise by £443 per year – or £36.91 per month. Neil Kenward of Ofgem said the rise was being driven by Donald Trump's war in the Middle East and as the rise – coming into force on January 1 – was confirmed, consumer bodies called for urgent action to help those struggling with their energy bills during the cold days. Anne McDonald, 72, said she only puts her heating on when her young grandson comes to visit and relies on hot water bottles and extra clothing to keep warm. Ian MacInnes, 77, said pensioners like him will already be dreading the new year and many will simply not be able to pay. They spoke out as they joined a protest against the “grotesque” hike in Glasgow city centre on Wednesday. Ian, from Glasgow’s south side, described the hike as “criminal”. He said: “After Christmas, what is there to look forward to? Even more debt yet again from extortionate fuel bills. “It impacts everyone because you’re watching every penny. It’s very basic things like, are you going to leave a light on? Do I heat this room or that one? It can’t go on like this. “This time around people will not be able to pay these bills. They’ll not be able to scrape around and find the money. “People are being driven into poverty This austerity and cost of living is ridiculous and it’s almost like it’s becoming normalised. “It’s just not good enough and people are going to rightly rebel against it. “We need Government action to intervene so people’s lives are not made into a ruinous situation.” Retired language teacher Anne, from Glasgow’s Dennistoun, said: “As a pensioner, it’s already very difficult to get by, especially in winter. I don’t put my heating on, in great part to save me money, but I really resent how the energy companies are thieving from people who don’t have much. “I use hot water bottles and put lots of clothes on. I try to keep it off as much as possible but have to heat my water for baths and showers." Anne said she was angry that "unjust" wars were to blame for the escalating problem. She said: “What we need is more money for people here in Scotland." Sean Clerkin, of the Scottish Tenants Association, is on Universal Credit and says he will not pay his bills in the new year. He organised the protest to stand against profiteering by energy firms, saying the hike was being driven by war and calling for Government intervention. The 65-year-old, from Barrhead, wants to see more windfall taxes imposed on energy firms to impose a price freeze and a system of social tariffs brought in to protect people on lower incomes. He said: “A lot of people will be reduced to cold, they’ll be hungry and they’ll be destitute in the new year. That’s what’s going to happen. “When people are in a desperate situation there will be civil unrest. We don’t want that to happen. We want Andy Burnham as our Prime Minister to come in and give the help that’s needed. “Me personally - I will not be paying my gas and electricity in the new year. Because I won’t be able to afford it and that’s the truth.” John Swinney has said he is “horrified” by the “staggering” projected price hike, saying it is a “complete failure of the Labour Government”. UK Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets for too long and the majority of households will get £100 towards their energy costs next year. news.title: MAGA Melts Down at Cape Cod Principal in Christmas Freakout
news.text:
MAGA influencers, who have long complained about a supposed “War on Christmas,” were quick to condemn the initiative.

“Principal of Harwich Elementary School in MA… just sent a memo to families and staff to maintain a “holiday free environment” during the Christmas season in order to create a ‘safe space for every student,’” Libs of TikTok, operated by conservative activist Chaya Raichik, wrote. “DEI destroys everything.”

The memo was sent to school staff, not families, despite Libs of TikTok’s claim.

Libs of TikTok also shared the principal’s photo and school email address. The post quickly garnered hundreds of thousands of views.

A social media account using the name “Maga Conservative Dr Ken Dabb” also criticised the memo.

“Christmas trees, wreaths and Santa imagery are out. Generic winter themes are encouraged instead, as if December in America were just a weather event,” he wrote. “A public school principal now treats the country’s biggest family holiday as a threat to be managed… Christmas is not a hazard. It is part of American life, and no memo from a principal’s office gets to erase it from a public school.”

The posts have been reposted dozens of times across social media, with many encouraging members of the public to contact the elementary school’s administration en masse to protest the policy.

Some local parents have pushed back against the policy, arguing that inclusivity means teaching children about and celebrating different December traditions rather than eliminating them altogether.

Abby McGillen, the parent of a fourth-grader, told Boston 25 News she believed the school should celebrate and teach students about diverse cultural traditions rather than cancel December festivities.

“We have a very small student body and a very diverse student body, and to be inclusive, that’s not to cancel traditions and cancel different cultures and learnings of all these different traditions of all these children from different backgrounds; it’s to celebrate them and teach these children,” she said.

The Monomoy Regional School District said no holiday ban had been introduced and no official policies had changed. The memo was intended to reaffirm its “commitment to be culturally responsive and aware, and to foster a deep sense of belonging for all in our community,” while maintaining support for seasonal celebrations and diverse traditions.

Among those who have promoted the notion of a “War on Christmas” is Donald Trump, who claimed during a visit to the Philippines this month that he had “ended” it back in 2016.

“[The Philippines] didn’t talk about taking Christmas away,” Trump said. “In our country, they said, ‘let’s not use Christmas anymore’ and in 2016, we ended that. That was ended.” 

But that hasn’t stopped MAGA influencers from airing their grievances online. 

“A Massachusetts elementary school has banned Christmas,” wrote conservative author Todd Starnes.
news.summary:
Jonathan Ernst / Jonathan Ernst/REUTERSA Massachusetts elementary school has become the latest subject of MAGA’s Christmas crusade. 

A memo sent by Harwich Elementary School’s principal to staff last week instructed teachers to maintain a “holiday-free environment,” removing Christmas, Hanukkah and other religious decorations from the building, according to local news outlet Boston 25. The memo said the move was intended to make students at the Cape Cod school feel included, while allowing winter-themed activities to continue.

MAGA influencers, who have long complained about a supposed “War on Christmas,” were quick to condemn the initiative.

news.title: Trump proposes new tariffs for India, China, and Bangladesh: Why is Pakistan spared?
news.text:
Donald Trump is back with his tariffs. The United States president has announced a fresh tariff proposal on 14 trading partners, including India, China and Bangladesh. China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40 per cent; Vietnam is second with up to 35 per cent, with others facing either 20 per cent or 25 per cent.
But there is one country that happened to be the trading partner of the US and yet is exempt from the fresh tariffs: Pakistan.
The countries that will face the fresh tariffs are: China, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam and the European Union.
But why has Trump proposed these tariffs, and why is Pakistan not on the list? We explain.
Trump fresh tariff proposal on India, China and Bangladesh
On Wednesday (November 25), the Trump administration proposed fresh import tariffs on 14 major trading partners, including India, China and Bangladesh, citing alleged excess industrial capacity and unfair trade practices.
The move came after a months-long investigation the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) launched in March 2026 under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974.
Washington alleged that government subsidies and manufacturing policies in these economies have encouraged production beyond market demand, creating global oversupply and hurting American manufacturers.
The investigation covered industries such as batteries, cement, chemicals and processed food. The Trump administration argues that excess manufacturing capacity and export-oriented production in foreign economies allow goods to enter international markets at lower prices, putting US producers at a disadvantage.
 The move came after a months-long investigation the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) launched in March 2026 under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974. Image used for representational purposes/AFP
The proposed tariffs are part of Washington’s effort to protect domestic industries and rebuild its trade framework after the US Supreme Court struck down Trump’s earlier sweeping tariffs in February 2026.
Under the proposed framework, India faces additional tariffs of up to 25 per cent, which could fall to 17 per cent if New Delhi reaches an Agreement on Reciprocal Trade with Washington. China faces an additional proposed duty of up to 20 per cent, potentially taking its overall tariff burden to 40 per cent.
Bangladesh faces proposed tariffs of up to 20 per cent. The 14 economies covered are China, India, Bangladesh, Cambodia, Indonesia, Japan, South Korea, Malaysia, Singapore, Switzerland, Taiwan, Thailand, Vietnam and the European Union.
These are proposals and not tariffs that have already come into force. The measures will undergo public consultation before the US administration finalises them.
A decision could come as early as January 2027.
Why Pakistan is not on Trump's list
Pakistan has been left out of the latest proposed tariff package despite being among the economies examined by the United States.
Mexico and Norway were also investigated but have not been included in the proposed additional levies.
A key explanation is Pakistan’s export composition. Its shipments to the US are concentrated largely in textiles and clothing, whereas the investigation has focused on industrial sectors such as steel, aluminium, automobiles, machinery and electronics.
Pakistan’s manufacturing and export profile therefore differs from the sectors that Washington has particularly scrutinised for excess production.
Pakistan’s exclusion does not mean that Washington has exempted it from all trade restrictions. The country continues to face existing US import duties, including a separate additional 10 per cent levy imposed in July 2026.
 Pakistan has been left out of the latest proposed tariff package despite being among the economies examined by the United States. File image/AFP
How Pakistan’s exports differ from its regional rivals
Pakistan’s exports to the US are heavily dependent on textiles and apparel. According to a Pakistan Textile Council assessment, textile and apparel products accounted for 82 per cent of Pakistan’s total exports to the US, worth approximately $5.614 billion in 2024.
The four major categories were knitted clothing, made-up textile articles, non-knitted clothing and cotton products.
The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics’ FY2023-24 trade report also highlights the dominance of textiles in its exports to the American market.
Knitwear accounted for $1.47 billion, readymade garments for $1.059 billion, bedwear for $581 million, made-up textile products for $439 million and towels for $368 million. Other exports included surgical goods, medical instruments, plastic materials, leather products and sports goods.
The concentration is different from the manufacturing profile of some of its regional competitors.
China has a substantial presence in industrial exports, including steel, electric vehicles and solar products. India’s manufacturing and export base includes automobiles, machinery, chemicals and electronics, alongside textiles.
 The Pakistan Bureau of Statistics’ FY2023-24 trade report also highlights the dominance of textiles in its exports to the American market. File image/AFP
These are among the sectors that have attracted particular scrutiny under the US investigation into excess industrial capacity.
What tariffs Pakistan already faces in the US
On July 23, Trump directed the imposition of a 10 per cent tariff on Pakistani goods under a separate Section 301 investigation concerning forced-labour import restrictions.
The measure took effect on July 24, subject to specified product exemptions. This is separate from the latest investigation into excess industrial capacity.
The US Trade Representative’s determination specifically accused Pakistan of failing to effectively enforce its prohibition on imports produced using forced labour. The official determination stated that Pakistan had “failed to effectively enforce its forced labor import prohibition”. The US subsequently imposed the 10 per cent duty on Pakistani products, with exemptions for specified goods.
Pakistan's ties with Washington
Pakistan has made considerable efforts to rebuild its relationship with Washington during Trump’s second presidency.
On September 25, 2025, when Trump hosted Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir at the White House, Sharif sought greater American investment in Pakistan, particularly in agriculture, technology, mining and energy.
The relationship has also expanded into trade, investment and security cooperation.
 On September 25, 2025, when Trump hosted Pakistani Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir at the White House, Sharif sought greater American investment in Pakistan, particularly in agriculture, technology, mining and energy. File image/AFP
On February 23 this year, Sharif met US Secretary of State Marco Rubio on the sidelines of the inaugural Board of Peace meeting in Washington. Both sides agreed to strengthen bilateral trade and economic activities, alongside cooperation in counterterrorism.
Pakistan also expressed satisfaction with the positive trajectory of its strategic relationship with the US under Trump’s leadership.

news.title: Judge declines to issue a long-term ban on taxpayer-funded, pro-Trump ads critics called propaganda
news.text: NEW YORK: A federal judge on Wednesday sided against Democrats on the federal government’s taxpayer-funded ads that promoted partisan messages and President Donald Trump ahead of the midterm elections, declining to extend a temporary ban.The Democratic National Committee had argued the TV spots were illegal government-sponsored propaganda intended to promote the president’s campaign message just weeks before November’s midterm elections. The ruling by U.S. District Judge Loren AliKhan comes after another judge in a similar case in New York also declined a long-term ban on the ads.AliKhan noted that a previous temporary restraining order against the ads had been issued when the election was less than a week away.“But the November 2026 midterm elections have come and gone,” she wrote, adding that the DNC was now claiming the party could be harmed by the ads in December congressional runoff elections or even because the 2028 presidential cycle has already begun.AliKhan took issue with the DNC's argument that the “permanent” nature of campaigns justified an injunction against the ads.“Such an argument, taken to its logical conclusion, would allow the DNC to seek preliminary relief in perpetuity because it could always point to the occurrence of some election somewhere in the country,” she wrote..Democrats sued the Trump administration in October after it began airing ads that were paid for at least in part by a $20 million Department of Homeland Security contract. In court papers, the DNC challenged at least 11 government-created ads that either aired on TV or appeared on Trump administration social media feeds.Some of the ads glorified the president with highlight reels of scenic speeches, promoted his tax cuts and emphasized support for law enforcement. One of them repurposed a clip that had been used by Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign, showing him walking down a hallway as his voice can be heard warning of a “final battle” against “globalists” and “warmongers.”A spokesperson for the DNC, Angelo Fernández Hernández, said in a statement that the organization was “disappointed” by the judge’s decision, adding that the DNC “will fight on to put an end to the Trump administration’s attempts to undermine our democracy.”The White House did not immediately respond to a request for comment.AliKhan in the earlier temporary restraining order blocked the Trump administration from developing, airing or distributing some of the challenged ads through Nov. 25. In the separate case in New York, the judge blocked a broader collection of the advertisements and required the government to pull three of them from official government websites and social media sites.While she declined to extend her ban against the ads, AliKhan said the DNC was likely to succeed on its claim that the use of public money for the ads violated the law.The White House has defended the ads as public service announcements akin to what past administrations have made to promote various policies. But the recent ads differ from many past public service announcements because they don’t try to help the public benefit from specific government programs, the plaintiffs have argued.Ahead of the ruling, the Justice Department argued in court papers that there was no threat of harm because the government had already ceased using public funds to air the ads and the midterm elections had passed..Follow The New Indian Express channel on WhatsApp Download the TNIE app to stay with us and follow the latest

news.title: US officials divided over Chinese spying allegations following Jensen Huang's return
news.text:
Days after President Donald Trump declared Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not a security threat to the United States, a central question remains unanswered: was the woman Huang ​was having an affair with a Chinese spy?

Senior US national security officials, including at the White House, FBI and the CIA, have debated that question in recent days in an effort to ‌determine if Alice Huang — a former executive at a major Nvidia customer — was working for or passing information to China’s premier spy agency, according to five people familiar with the matter, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.

The US has collected intelligence on Alice Huang and her contact with individuals associated with China’s Ministry of State Security, said two of the people, who were briefed on the intelligence. That intelligence has been described for months in reports from several intelligence agencies, including the CIA, the people said.

Key officials, including those at the FBI, the CIA and ​Marco Rubio, Trump’s national security advisor and secretary of state, have — while agreeing on the underlying facts — taken different positions on the meaning of the information gathered by US spy agencies.

Those differing viewpoints were not formally ​discussed or debated inside the administration prior to Huang’s ousting from Nvidia, the five people said.

The interpretation of the facts is important for understanding Trump’s decision to push for ⁠Huang’s reinstatement as CEO of Nvidia, three of the people said. The intelligence will likely be central to any congressional investigation into Nvidia and the president’s actions.

Reuters could not determine the details of the intelligence reports.

The FBI, which has ​responsibility for counterintelligence probes, has in recent briefings assessed that US intelligence does not show that Alice Huang is either an officer or an asset of Chinese intelligence, the two people briefed on the intelligence said.

The CIA’s view is more nuanced. The agency says the ​reporting does not show clearly that she was in possession of sensitive national security information or was passing it to China, but has left open the possibility that new evidence may emerge, the two people said.

Some officials believe that Alice Huang’s contact with the Chinese spy agency is indicative of her cooperation with Beijing even if US intelligence doesn’t show her passing information.

A classified memo written by Rubio earlier this year indicated that the MSS had recruited Huang, potentially as an asset, according to an earlier New York ​Times report.

The intelligence reports were held closely inside the intelligence community and among cabinet officials. They were not shared with Congress, the two people said.

The White House, CIA, FBI and State Department declined to comment. Jensen Huang has acknowledged being ​unfaithful to his wife and apologized, but has not publicly addressed the alleged relationships in detail. China has denied the espionage allegations. Attempts by Reuters to reach Alice Huang have been unsuccessful.

Intelligence not widely shared

The different interpretations of US intelligence highlight what ‌current and former ⁠intelligence officials say has become a problem for the Trump administration: classified information is now less widely shared and debated inside the intelligence community.

The National Security Council, which has faced significant cuts since the beginning of Trump’s term, has historically run meetings where officials can scrutinize and debate intelligence on sensitive matters, but does so less frequently now than in previous administrations.

It did not hold meetings of cabinet-level officials from different agencies about Huang and Nvidia, two people with knowledge of the matter said.

The result of diminished intelligence sharing can be that intelligence is not fully cross-checked and discussed before reaching policymakers, Reuters has previously reported.

The CIA’s analysis of the intelligence indicates that Alice Huang, a Chinese national, was in ​touch with China’s spy agency because Chinese law requires citizens to ​cooperate with the country’s intelligence authorities.

One of the ⁠people said CIA reporting on the matter focused mainly on Alice Huang’s role at her former employer, Megaspeed, and its diversion of US chips to China. Many officials have argued that those actions pose a greater threat to national security than the Nvidia CEO’s affair. Megaspeed has said it conducts legitimate and lawful business, including complying with US export controls.

Competing narratives

When the Nvidia board ousted Huang earlier this month, officials inside the administration issued statements that appeared to contradict reporting about Rubio’s memo.

Vice President JD Vance and Trump, both of ​whom have spoken favorably about ⁠the Nvidia CEO, said after speaking with Attorney General Todd Blanche that they had determined the CEO was not a national security threat.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said it was unclear whether Alice Huang was an asset of the Chinese spy services.

Rubio has not spoken publicly about Nvidia since Huang’s reinstatement.

When the New York Times broke the news about that memo earlier this month, it caused uproar inside the administration and among board members of Nvidia who questioned whether Huang knew he ⁠was having an ​affair with someone who was passing information to China, according to two people familiar with the the conversations.

Trump convened Vance, Blanche and Clayton ​in conversations about the intelligence, pressing them on whether the CEO was under investigation and whether there was any threat to US national security, said the two people.

Blanche told Vance that Huang posed no threat, as Reuters has previously reported. Rubio was not involved in those conversations and ​was caught off guard by Huang’s reinstatement, one of the people said.

The State Department did not respond to questions about Rubio’s involvement in the conversations.

news.title: Abdul El-Sayed rips Trump — in Thanksgiving message about unity
news.text:
Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed accused President Trump of tearing the nation apart Wednesday in a Thanksgiving message about finding common ground with family at the dinner table. 

The Michigan Democrat called Thanksgiving “an opportunity to come together and break bread with people with whom you might not have had a lot of conversations in the past,” in a video message posted on X. 

“And sometimes those conversations can get, well, a little bit spicier than the Thanksgiving meal, and I know that this has caused a lot of anxiety,” El-Sayed continued. 

The newly-elected senator then blamed Trump for being the “reason why” some family members haven’t spoken to each other in years or are nervous about spending Turkey Day together. 

“You know, Donald Trump has one neat trick,” El-Sayed argued. “It’s the ability to tear us apart, to become the subject of every conversation, and to force us to take sides.” 

“And I think it’s really important for us, as an exercise in healing our civics, to find the places that we agree,” he added. 

In the middle of his message, El-Sayed shoe-horned his pitch for government-run healthcare – a topic he’s keen on discussing directly with Trump. 

“You might believe in ‘Medicare for all’ because you believe in empathy, but you might also believe in ‘Medicare for all’ because you believe in duty,” he said, “but I think it’s by finding the least common denominator, the things that we agree on, that help us to address where we disagree in a much more agreeable way.” 

On Tuesday, Trump told The Post he plans to meet with El-Sayed to discuss passing “Medicare for all,” which the senator-elect is willing to rebrand as “Trumpcare.” 

“Maybe there’s some place in the middle that we could go,” the president said of the potential for passing single-payer healthcare legislation. 

El-Sayed, meanwhile, told Politico’s Playbook he’s “looking forward to a conversation” with Trump about healthcare.

“Even President Trump understands that something’s got to be done,” he added.
