news.title: Nvidia-led $2 trillion chip rally unravels. What comes next for Wall Street?
news.text:
Wall Street's historic rally in semiconductor stocks is losing momentum, with investors once again questioning the sustainability of the artificial intelligence boom just days after Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang returned to the company's leadership. The chip sector has given back more than half of the gains made during Monday's record-breaking rebound, raising concerns that the latest market recovery could give way to another round of selling.
The sell-off has also unsettled global markets, although Asian stocks staged a recovery on Thursday, as investors assessed the latest US tariff proposals and took a break from the recent technology stock rout. Japan's Nikkei rose 1.6 per cent, South Korea's benchmark index gained 1.9 per cent and Taiwan's market advanced 1.4 per cent. The broader Asia-Pacific index excluding Japan climbed 1.5 per cent.
European markets also signalled a recovery, with EURO STOXX 50 futures rising 2.3 per cent, while futures for the S&P 500 and Nasdaq gained 0.6 per cent and 0.8 per cent, respectively.
The rebound followed a bruising few sessions for semiconductor stocks. A basket of 62 semiconductor companies, tracked by Yahoo Finance, added nearly $2 trillion in market value on Monday after Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO, following intervention by US President Donald Trump. Nvidia alone accounted for approximately $950 billion of the gains, marking the biggest single-day increase in market value recorded by a company.
But the optimism proved short-lived. The Philadelphia Semiconductor Index (SOX) plunged nearly 8 per cent on Tuesday, with chipmakers Micron, Advanced Micro Devices (AMD) and Intel losing between 8 per cent and 11 per cent. Broadcom and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC) also declined around 4 per cent.
The selling pressure continued on Wednesday, when the semiconductor index briefly fell below its previous Friday's low. Nvidia shares dropped as much as 9 per cent during the session, while Micron fell as much as 13 per cent, before investors stepped in to limit the losses.
The weakness also spread beyond semiconductor companies. The S&P 500 fell more than 3 per cent during Wednesday's trading session, while the Nasdaq 100 declined nearly 5 per cent at one point. Both indices recovered most of their losses by the close, although major technology companies, including Alphabet, Microsoft and Amazon, ended lower.
Why is Wall Street losing confidence in the AI rally?
The return of Huang has settled questions surrounding Nvidia's leadership, but it has done little to address the bigger concerns confronting investors. The central question is whether the enormous investments being made in artificial intelligence infrastructure will eventually generate sufficient returns.
Technology companies are spending heavily on advanced chips, data centres and computing infrastructure to support the development and deployment of AI models. Much of this expansion is also being supported by borrowing, making the sector vulnerable to rising financing costs.
Luke Kawa of Sherwood News told Yahoo Finance's Market Hang that the latest sell-off was not driven by one particular development but reflected the accumulation of concerns that investors had been highlighting for some time.
Nvidia also faces questions about its corporate governance and leadership. S&P has placed the chipmaker's credit rating on watch for a possible downgrade, citing concerns about weaknesses in its management and board. The development has added to investor unease at a time when the company is already facing scrutiny over its business and political developments.
Nvidia shares ended Wednesday down 3.9 per cent at $149.30, leaving them well below their October peak of $243.37.
What does history say about the next market move?
Historical market patterns offer another reason for investors to remain cautious.
An analysis by Yahoo Finance examined 20 instances since 1993 when the SPDR S&P 500 ETF (SPY), which tracks the broader US stock market, opened a Monday trading session at least 2 per cent higher.
In five of those instances, the ETF surrendered at least half of its Monday gains by Wednesday's close. Yahoo Finance found that all five subsequently fell below the previous Friday's low within three months, with most recording the decline within a week.
In comparison, among the 15 instances when the initial rally held up, only around a third eventually fell below the previous Friday's low within the same period.
The previous Friday's low for the S&P 500 in the current episode stood at approximately 6,883.
The historical comparison suggests that if the latest rebound continues to lose momentum, US equities could face further downside in the coming weeks.
However, the longer-term picture is not entirely bearish. Yahoo Finance found that the S&P 500 ETF was higher one year later in 17 of the 20 historical instances examined.
Could the AI trade recover in the longer term?
The current market situation also draws comparisons with 2018, when the Federal Reserve continued raising interest rates even as US equities experienced a sharp correction.
The central bank eventually paused its rate increases, and stocks recovered to record levels by April.
Alfonso Peccatiello of Macro Compass sees similarities with that period but believes markets could experience further weakness before a sustained recovery begins. He has pointed towards the possibility of the S&P 500 falling towards 6,500.
The semiconductor sector has already surrendered a substantial portion of its gains made during 2026, with the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index falling below levels that had acted as a ceiling earlier in the year.
Investors are now looking for clarity on whether the AI infrastructure boom can sustain its pace of expansion and deliver the earnings growth needed to justify the money being poured into it.
Will the Federal Reserve raise interest rates?
The prospect of higher interest rates in the United States is adding to the uncertainty. Markets are still expecting the Federal Reserve to raise borrowing costs at its December meeting, even as the recent stock market volatility has prompted questions about how aggressively the central bank will tighten monetary policy.
The latest personal consumption expenditures (PCE) report, the US central bank's preferred inflation gauge, showed core prices rising 3.3 per cent year-on-year, higher than expected. Meanwhile, US economic growth for the third quarter was revised upwards to 4.3 per cent.
According to Reuters, interest rate futures indicate a 98 per cent probability of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December. However, expectations of a larger half-percentage-point increase have faded.
US Treasury yields also declined to multi-week lows on Wednesday despite the stronger economic growth and persistent inflation. The yield on the 10-year Treasury note touched an 11-week low before recovering to around 4.848 per cent.
Bond investors are increasingly considering whether global equity market losses and concerns about the sustainability of AI-driven business investment could eventually influence central banks' decisions.
Higher interest rates could make financing more expensive for companies expanding their AI infrastructure and put additional pressure on technology stocks that have benefited from high valuations.
What investors will watch next
The immediate focus is likely to shift towards Nvidia's upcoming Senate testimony on December 3. Investors will be watching Huang's appearance for clarity on the company's position amid the broader scrutiny surrounding its business and political developments.
The Federal Reserve's December 9 interest-rate decision will be another crucial event for markets, particularly as persistent inflation could keep borrowing costs elevated.
Advisors Capital Management's Gus Scacco told Yahoo Finance that markets could remain in a period of uncertainty while investors wait for Huang's testimony and assess the next developments.
The latest reversal shows that resolving Nvidia's leadership uncertainty is not enough to restore confidence in the broader AI trade. Whether chip stocks can regain their momentum will depend on a combination of corporate earnings, AI spending returns, borrowing costs and the direction of US monetary policy.

news.title: Gold steadies after hitting over 1-year low; Fed outlook in focus
news.text:
Gold prices steadied on Thursday after the ‌previous session’s plunge to a more than one-year low, as hot US inflation data reinforced expectations of Federal Reserve interest rate hikes.

Spot gold was little changed at $3,580.87 per ounce by 0317 ​GMT.

Bullion briefly fell below the key $3,500 level on Wednesday for the first time ​since September 2025.

US gold futures for December delivery gained 1.2% to $3,578.70.

“Investors ⁠are covering shorts going into a major US holiday, which is driving the ​price action in gold today,” said Ilya Spivak, head of global macro at ​Tastylive.

“Gold continues to be sold to raise cash in this sentiment sensitive environment amid risk aversion,” he added.

The US economy grew much faster than initially estimated in the third quarter, while inflation ​increased further in October, reinforcing expectations that the Fed will raise rates next month ​and again in early 2027.

The US central bank last raised interest rates in September.

A Fed survey showed that economic ‌growth ⁠persisted at a “slight to moderate” pace across most of the US in recent weeks, while inflation remained sticky and employment levels rose.

Higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding non-yielding bullion, reducing its appeal to investors.

Asian shares meanwhile ​dug out a rare rally ​after Wall Street ⁠fought back from deep lows, though concerns over the circular financing of AI and a new round of US ​tariffs made for a muted mood in a holiday-thinned session.

US ​President Donald ⁠Trump fired a new tariff salvo on Wednesday at 14 major trading partners including China, Japan and the European Union, undeterred in his protectionist push by the losses ⁠his Republican ​Party suffered in US midterm elections.

Among other metals, ​spot silver rose 1% to $41.64 per ounce, platinum gained 1.6% to $1,301.33 and palladium climbed 2.1% to $880.50.
